Abstract:
<jats:p>The autonomous flight capability of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in complex dynamic environments highly depends on the accurate perception of the environment and their own state by onboard sensors. However, limited by sensor noise, model mismatch, observation heterogeneity, and external environmental disturbances, the output of onboard sensors inherently possesses significant uncertainty and randomness. How to transform imperfect, multi-source, and asynchronous sensor observations into reliable state estimation and environmental cognition results through statistical modeling and inference methods has become one of the core issues in UAV perception system research. This paper systematically reviews the development of research related to UAV onboard sensors from a statistical perspective, focusing on the application and evolution of statistical modeling, state estimation, and multi-sensor fusion methods in UAV perception systems. First, it summarizes the typical statistical observation models and noise characteristics of inertial sensors, satellite navigation, vision, lidar, and novel neuromorphic sensors, and analyzes key statistical issues such as random walk, non-Gaussian noise, and time-dependent errors. Subsequently, based on the Bayesian state estimation framework, this paper systematically reviews the application progress of Kalman filtering, error state filtering, particle filtering, and robust statistical methods in UAV navigation and localization, and compares and analyzes the statistical nature of loosely coupled and tightly coupled multi-sensor fusion strategies. Building upon this, it further discusses joint probabilistic modeling methods for heterogeneous sensors such as vision, inertial, and radar, as well as the fusion trend of statistical learning and deep models in high-dimensional perception tasks. Finally, this paper summarizes the role and limitations of statistical methods in UAV airborne sensor research and looks forward to future development directions oriented towards uncertainty perception (the capability to explicitly quantify the reliability of perception results), risk-constrained decision-making (strategies that incorporate estimation variance into control loops to ensure operational safety), and integrated sensing-computing architectures.</jats:p>

                           Abstract

                            Physical access to robotic manipulators remains constrained by cost, safety requirements,
                       and limited laboratory availability, creating barriers to both research and education.
                           This paper presents a computational framework that combines stochastic error model-
                           ing with Digital Twin technology to characterize positioning uncertainty in a six-degree-
                          of-freedom manipulator without requiring physical hardware. Four independent noise
                           sources—joint encoder noise, thermal drift, elastic link deformation, and geometric param-
                                eter tolerances—are modeled as stochastic processes and propagated through the manipu-
                                lator kinematics using Monte Carlo simulation with N = 10,000 trials across 50 workspace
                             configurations. The results reveal that elastic deformation dominates the combined po-
                              sitioning error by a factor of 45.94 over encoder noise, contributing 99.97% of the total
                          root-mean-square (RMS) uncertainty. A probabilistic workspace map constructed from
                          3000 sampled configurations quantifies accuracy and manipulability across the reachable
                             space, exposing a counterintuitive trade-off: configurations with higher manipulability in-
                              dices tend to exhibit larger positioning errors due to gravitational loading on extended links.
                    Two control algorithms—a reverse process-based control law (RPBCL) and sliding mode
                              control (SMC)—are evaluated under stochastic conditions over 200 trials. SMC achieves a
                      mean steady-state error of 0.0029 mm, representing a 48.2% reduction compared to RPBCL
                              (0.0056 mm), with the difference confirmed statistically significant by a two-sample t-test
                                       (t = 5.066, p = 0.000002). All results are visualized through a Unity3D Digital Twin inter-
                             face that renders probabilistic workspace maps, three-dimensional error ellipsoids, and

                             1. Introduction

                           The deployment of robotic manipulators across manufacturing, medical, and educa-
                              tional settings has accelerated considerably over the past decade, driven by advances in
                            mechatronics, embedded computing, and control theory [1,2]. Despite this growth, the gap
                         between theoretical control design and physical implementation remains wide. Laborato-
                                  ries capable of hosting industrial-grade manipulators are expensive to equip and maintain,
                        and the operational risks associated with unvalidated control algorithms—collision, actua-
                                tor damage, injury—discourage experimental iteration [3]. These constraints are especially
                            acute in academic environments, where student-to-robot ratios are unfavorable and super-
                            vised access hours are limited.
                                   Digital Twin technology has emerged as a principled response to this problem. By
                          maintaining a continuously updated virtual replica of a physical system, a Digital Twin
                           enables simulation, monitoring, and predictive analysis without direct hardware interac-
                              tion [4,5]. This framework acts as an intelligent manufacturing system component within
                        an Industrial IoT (IIoT) infrastructure, where the cyber–physical integration of real-time
                    ROS messaging and virtual replica environments defines the smart space. The proposed
                               Digital Twin architecture aligns with the IoT-Enabled Smart Devices and Systems paradigm
                       by providing bidirectional data flow between the physical manipulator and its virtual
                             counterpart, enabling real-time monitoring, stochastic performance prediction, and control
                             validation within a smart manufacturing environment [4,5].
                                 In robotics, Digital Twins have been applied to trajectory planning, fault detection,
                       and operator training, with recent work demonstrating that high-fidelity kinematic and
                        dynamic models can reproduce physical robot behavior with sub-millimeter accuracy [6,7].
                      What remains less explored is the integration of stochastic uncertainty models within the
                              Digital Twin framework—that is, using the virtual replica not merely to replicate nominal
                             behavior, but to characterize the probabilistic envelope of positioning errors arising from
                            real-world noise sources.
                                  Positioning accuracy in robotic manipulators is affected by multiple concurrent uncer-
                               tainty sources. Joint encoder quantization and noise introduce angular measurement errors
                              that propagate nonlinearly through the forward kinematics [8]. Manufacturing tolerances
                       on link dimensions and joint axis orientations produce systematic geometric offsets that
                               persist across all configurations [9]. Thermal expansion of structural components during
                           sustained operation shifts the effective Denavit–Hartenberg parameters away from their
                              calibrated values [10]. Perhaps most significantly, elastic deformation of links under gravi-
                                tational and inertial loading introduces configuration-dependent deflections that can reach
                              tens of millimeters in extended poses [11,12]. These sources have been studied individually
                               in the literature, but their combined stochastic effect

                                 In addition to steady-state accuracy, dynamic performance metrics were extracted
                        from the convergence trajectories over 200 Monte Carlo trials. SMC achieves a mean rise
                          time of 0.18 ± 0.02 s (42% faster than RPBCL: 0.31 ± 0.04 s) and a mean settling time of
                               0.97 ± 0.14 s (32% shorter than RPBCL: 1.42 ± 0.21 s). Neither controller exhibits overshoot
                         under the applied saturation mechanisms (tanh for RPBCL, boundary layer approximation
                                for SMC). These results confirm that SMC outperforms RPBCL across all evaluated metrics:
                              steady-state accuracy, convergence speed, and settling time.
                            The superior performance of SMC is attributable to the invariance property of sliding
                     mode dynamics. Once the system reaches the sliding surface s = 0, bounded disturbances
                              satisfying ∥d∥< η are rejected without affecting the sliding behavior. The boundary
                              layer saturation function F(s) prevents chattering while preserving this rejection property,
                              resulting in more consistent final positioning across noise realizations. RPBCL, which
                             applies a smooth gradient correction proportional to the error, has no analogous rejection
                       mechanism and accumulates the effect of each noise realization independently.

                             4. Discussion

                           The results presented in this work carry several implications that extend beyond the
                                specific manipulator configuration studied.
                             Regarding uncertainty sources, the overwhelming dominance of elastic deforma-
                              tion (97% of combined error) challenges the conventional focus on encoder precision in
                          manipulator design.
                            While modern encoders achieve resolutions below 0.001 rad, the present analysis
                           demonstrates that such improvements yield negligible accuracy gains when link compliance
                          remains uncompensated. This finding is consistent with the stiffness identification work
                              of Alici and Shirinzadeh [11] and Dumas et al. [12], who independently identified elastic
                              deflection as the primary accuracy limitation in serial manipulators under gravitational
                             loading. The implication for engineering practice is direct: accuracy improvement budgets

The excerpt reports results only for the FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L; it provides no information about Kinova, UR5, Franka, ABB, or other low-cost robot arms. For the FANUC arm, analytical and Monte Carlo models agreed closely in compact and medium configurations, where errors were approximately normal and covariance estimates matched direct linearization. In the elongated configuration, nonlinear kinematic effects caused asymmetric and shifted error distributions. Experimental error ellipsoids showed that the major axis could be displaced by up to 10–11° relative to model predictions, with variance up to 20% higher than predicted. The study also constructed a workspace geometric-reliability map representing successful positioning probability. Reliability was approximately 0.98 in central workspace regions associated with compact configurations and declined toward the workspace boundaries, reaching low values around 0.70 in peripheral zones. The excerpt additionally reports that positioning accuracy degraded over time: average position error increased from 0.018 mm in the first three months to 0.041 mm in the last three months, while average orientation error rose from 0.28° to 0.71°. Thus, the provided passage supports detailed conclusions for FANUC only, not comparative results for the other named robot families.

The excerpt reports probabilistic positioning and reliability analysis only for the six-axis FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L; it does not mention Kinova, UR5, Franka, ABB, or low-cost robot arms, nor does it provide comparative results for those models using error ellipsoids or workspace-accuracy maps. For FANUC, Monte Carlo simulations incorporated stochastic DH-parameter and joint errors, nonlinear direct kinematics, complex permissible regions, correlated errors, and dependence on configuration and trajectory. The analysis produced a reliability map over joint-configuration space, allowing identification of more reliable postures and avoidance of singularity-prone regions. Independent errors in joints 4–6 were associated primarily with orientation errors, while correlated errors in joints 1–3 caused vertical or horizontal displacement of the working point. Correlated errors in DH parameters altered the spatial distribution of posture errors. The robot’s outstretched-arm configurations, particularly those with a large second-joint angle, showed significantly reduced reliability because of increased Jacobian sensitivity. The excerpt also notes that the robot has low independent drive errors, although thermal expansion can produce correlated errors. Monte Carlo was considered useful for complex configuration-dependent reliability assessment, despite high computational cost and the need for importance sampling in rare-event, low-reliability cases.

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table summarizing the software tools and libraries for robot positioning accuracy/repeatability visualization, with columns: Tool/Library, Language, Key Capabilities for Accuracy Visualization, Published Reference, Availability/Notes.

Tools to include:
1. pytransform3d - Python, SE(3) uncertainty propagation, 6D covariance composition (concat_locally_uncertain_transforms, concat_globally_uncertain_transforms), adjoint_from_transform, projected hyperellipsoid visualization, URDF kinematics, Matplotlib and Open3D backends. Reference: Fabisch & Popescu 2026, Frontiers in Robotics and AI, doi:10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457. Open source.
2. MATLAB + Unity3D Digital Twin - MATLAB for Monte Carlo simulation and covariance computation, Unity3D for interactive 3D error ellipsoid rendering and workspace map display. Reference: Makhambetov et al. 2026, doi:10.3390/electronics15143095.
3. RoboDK - Robot simulation and offline programming, ISO cube definition, target teaching. Used by Pollak 2023 for ISO 9283 measurement setup. No built-in statistical repeatability map.
4. Probabilistic Product-of-Exponentials (PPOE) - Lie-group-based probabilistic kinematics. Reference: Meyer et al. IROS 2022, doi:10.1109/iros47612.2022.9981399.
5. ROS/RViz - 3D visualization, transform frames, custom marker/mesh display for ellipsoids. Widely used research platform.
6. MATLAB Robotics Toolbox / NumPy + SciPy - General purpose kinematics and statistics for eigendecomposition, Monte Carlo."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Tool/Library | Language | Key Capabilities for Accuracy Visualization | Published Reference | Availability/Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **pytransform3d** | Python | Represents uncertain SE(3) transforms with 6×6 covariance; composes globally and locally uncertain transforms with `concat_globally_uncertain_transforms` and `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms`; changes covariance frames with `adjoint_from_transform`; projects 6D confidence hyperellipsoids into 3D; supports trajectory covariance, URDF kinematics, Matplotlib, and Open3D. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000044) | Fabisch & Popescu, *Frontiers in Robotics and AI* (2026), [doi:10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457) | Open-source Python library. Particularly suitable for an inexpensive, scriptable pipeline from URDF and measured covariance to ellipsoids along a trajectory. |
| **MATLAB + Unity3D Digital Twin** | MATLAB; C#/Unity | MATLAB performs Monte Carlo propagation, covariance/eigendecomposition, RMS and P95 calculations, and workspace sampling; Unity3D interactively renders color-coded probabilistic workspace point clouds, 3D error ellipsoids, and controller diagnostics. The published example used 10,000 trials at 50 configurations and a map of 3,000 configurations with 500 trials each. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000036) | Makhambetov et al., *Electronics* (2026), [doi:10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095) | MATLAB and Unity are separate products; Unity has free-use tiers, while MATLAB generally requires a license. The cited manipulator analysis is simulation-only, so its maps should not be treated as measured arm performance. |
| **RoboDK** | Python API; proprietary application | Robot simulation and offline programming; defines an ISO test cube and measurement plane, teaches targets on surfaces, generates point-visit programs, checks reachability, and visualizes nominal paths. Pollák and Goryl used it to prepare five ISO-style targets and separate X/Y measurement programs. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) | Pollák & Goryl, *Machines* (2023), [doi:10.3390/machines11070734](https://doi.org/10.3390/machines11070734) | Commercial software with educational/trial options. The cited evidence does **not** establish a built-in statistical repeatability-map or covariance-ellipsoid facility; export measurements to Python or MATLAB for those analyses. |
| **Probabilistic Product-of-Exponentials (PPOE)** | Mathematical model; research implementations commonly in C++/Python/MATLAB | Lie-group-based probabilistic kinematics that represents correlated, configuration-dependent errors and propagates them along a kinematic chain to a 6-DoF end-effector covariance. Demonstrated on a Kinova Jaco2 with AprilTag observations and VICON ground truth; suitable for configuration-dependent covariance or projected confidence-volume displays. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000042) | Meyer, Strobl & Triebel, IROS (2022), [doi:10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399](https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399) | A modeling method rather than a turnkey visualization application. A practical implementation path is PPOE covariance propagation followed by pytransform3d, Open3D, or RViz rendering. |
| **ROS / RViz** | C++; Python; ROS messages | ROS `tf`/`tf2` maintains frame relationships; RViz displays robot models, measured and commanded paths, point clouds, arrows, and custom marker or triangle meshes that can encode ellipsoids. It can serve as the live display layer for AprilTag-derived TCP samples and path-error overlays. pytransform3d’s `TransformManager` is explicitly inspired by ROS `tf`. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) | No dedicated peer-reviewed accuracy-map implementation was established in the retrieved evidence; related transformation and uncertainty functionality is documented by Fabisch & Popescu (2026), [doi:10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457) | Open source and well suited to live experiments. Ellipsoid fitting, confidence scaling, and repeatability statistics must be calculated in a separate node; RViz primarily renders the resulting markers. |
| **MATLAB Robotics Toolbox / NumPy + SciPy** | MATLAB or Python | General-purpose implementation route for forward kinematics, Jacobians, covariance estimation, eigendecomposition, Monte Carlo sampling, RMS/P95 statistics, interpolation, and ellipsoid meshes. The core operations are Σₓ = JΣqJᵀ and Σ = VDVᵀ, with confidence semi-axes derived from √λ. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000030) | The retrieved literature supports the underlying workflow in Makhambetov et al. (2026), [doi:10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095), and Issametova et al. (2026), [doi:10.3390/math14030580](https://doi.org/10.3390/math14030580) | NumPy/SciPy are open source; MATLAB and some toolboxes require licenses. No retrieved paper establishes a one-click repeatability-map function in either stack—the analysis must be assembled from their numerical and plotting primitives. |


*Table: Software and computational frameworks for turning measured or modeled robot-position errors into ellipsoids, workspace maps, and trajectory-error displays. The notes distinguish turnkey visualization features from tools that require custom statistical processing.*

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'

Abstract:
In this paper, we present a quantitative performance investigation and repeatability assessment of a mobile robotic system for 3D mapping. With the aim of a more efficient and automatic data acquisition process with respect to well-established manual topographic operations, a 3D laser scanner coupled with an inertial measurement unit is installed on a mobile platform and used to perform a high-resolution mapping of the surrounding environment. Point clouds obtained with the use of a mobile robot are compared with those acquired with the device carried manually as well as with a terrestrial laser scanner survey that serves as a ground truth. Experimental results show that both mapping modes provide similar accuracy and repeatability, whereas the robotic system compares favorably with respect to the handheld modality in terms of noise level and point distribution. The outcomes demonstrate the feasibility of the mobile robotic platform as a promising technology for automatic and accurate 3D mapping.

Abstract:
Planar fiducial markers are commonly used to estimate a pose of a camera relative to the marker. This information can be combined with other sensor data to provide a global or local position estimate of the system in the environment using a state estimator such as the Kalman filter. To achieve accurate estimates, the observation noise covariance matrix must be properly configured to reflect the sensor output’s characteristics. However, the observation noise of the pose obtained from planar fiducial markers varies across the measurement range and this fact needs to be taken into account during the sensor fusion to provide a reliable estimate. In this work, we present experimental measurements of the fiducial markers in real and simulation scenarios for 2D pose estimation. Based on these measurements, we propose analytical functions that approximate the variances of pose estimates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a 2D robot localisation experiment, where we present a method for estimating covariance model parameters based on user measurements and a technique for fusing pose estimates from multiple markers.

The main objective of the present paper was to verify the repeatability of the Panasonic TM-2000 welding robot at a manufacturing company. Abstract:
For the measurement and technical evaluation of industrial robots, a test procedure defined in ISO 9283 has existed for 25 years, with which the performance criteria of industrial robots relevant to users, e.g., path accuracy, pose accuracy, or position overshoot, can be measured. The specified test procedure and defined operating and environmental conditions are to be adhered to enable comparability of the tested robotic systems. In the production environment, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly being utilized for tasks such as material transportation and surveillance. However, for these applications, which are currently the subject of considerable discussion, UAVs must also adhere to industrial standards regarding performance criteria. To ensure that these performance criteria are met across all manufacturers, a defined test procedure for UAVs is required in which all relevant performance criteria can be determined based on ISO 9283. This article will, therefore, first conduct the test procedure for a UAV under ISO 9283 and examine the transferability of the standard for performance measurement of UAVs in detail. However, evaluating the measurements suggests that the procedure defined in ISO 9283 is not fully transferable to UAVs as measurements do not fully cover the potential strengths or weaknesses of UAVs regarding the test procedure. The article concludes by discussing modifications to the test procedure and thus suggesting establishing a standardized procedure for UAVs. This procedure should enable the acquisition of performance criteria and might function as a safety benchmark before operating UAVs.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Physical access to robotic manipulators remains constrained by cost, safety requirements, and limited laboratory availability, creating barriers to both research and education. This paper presents a computational framework that combines stochastic error modeling with Digital Twin technology to characterize positioning uncertainty in a six-degree-of-freedom manipulator without requiring physical hardware. Four independent noise sources—joint encoder noise, thermal drift, elastic link deformation, and geometric parameter tolerances—are modeled as stochastic processes and propagated through the manipulator kinematics using Monte Carlo simulation with N = 10,000 trials across 50 workspace configurations. The results reveal that elastic deformation dominates the combined positioning error by a factor of 45.94 over encoder noise, contributing 99.97% of the total root-mean-square (RMS) uncertainty. A probabilistic workspace map constructed from 3000 sampled configurations quantifies accuracy and manipulability across the reachable space, exposing a counterintuitive trade-off: configurations with higher manipulability indices tend to exhibit larger positioning errors due to gravitational loading on extended links. Two control algorithms—a reverse process-based control law (RPBCL) and sliding mode control (SMC)—are evaluated under stochastic conditions over 200 trials. SMC achieves a mean steady-state error of 0.0029 mm, representing a 48.2% reduction compared to RPBCL (0.0056 mm), with the difference confirmed statistically significant by a two-sample t-test (t = 5.066, p = 0.000002). All results are visualized through a Unity3D Digital Twin interface that renders probabilistic workspace maps, three-dimensional error ellipsoids, and a real-time sliding surface monitor. The proposed framework provides a foundation for safe, hardware-free evaluation of manipulator control strategies in engineering education and research.</jats:p>

Abstract:
We present prior knowledge robot keypoint detection (PK-ROKED), a learning-based pipeline for probabilistic robot pose estimation relative to a camera, addressing inaccuracies in forward kinematics, particularly in systems with elastic and lightweight modules. Our approach integrates a probabilistic 2-D keypoint detection mechanism that leverages prior knowledge derived from the robot’s imprecise kinematics. We further improve the detection accuracy and geometric understanding by incorporating segmentation of the robot arm. The method computes reliable uncertainty estimates, enabling a robust 2D–6D fusion for precise robot arm pose estimation from a single detected keypoint. PK-ROKED requires only synthetic training data, effectively exploits imperfect kinematics as valuable prior knowledge, and introduces a novel fusion framework for enhanced robot pose estimation. We validate our method on the Panda-Orb dataset, demonstrating competitive performance against state-of-the-art approaches. In addition, we evaluate on two other robotic systems in real-world scenarios and show its practicality by using the predictions to initialize a tracking algorithm. Code and pretrained models are available.

Abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Rigid transformations in three dimensions (3D) are fundamental tools in robotics, computer vision and graphics, and physics simulation. However, there are many pitfalls for practitioners: various alternative representations of rigid transformations and uncertainty, each with its own competing conventions, sometimes without clear documentation, ambiguities in representations, singularities, and difficulties in handling many transformations in complex systems. This article presents the new features of
                    <jats:monospace>pytransform3d</jats:monospace>
                    , a Python library for working with rigid transformations in 3D that helps tackle these difficulties. Specifically, we show applications of its new batch data processing functions, uncertainty propagation, and 3D visualization. Furthermore, we present applications of its transformation graph
                    <jats:monospace>TransformManager</jats:monospace>
                    , a tool inspired by tf of the Robot Operating System (ROS), which has a subclass for loading robot kinematics and a new subclass that handles time-varying transformations. In examples from imitation learning, kinematics, state estimation, and log data processing, we demonstrate these features and show that only a few lines of code are sufficient to solve these complex problems correctly. The explicit terminology of the library makes this code readable and reviewable. The library has 100% test coverage of its core features, has a broader feature set than comparable libraries, and handles batch processing of spatial data in fewer lines of code and faster than its alternatives.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:

 Robotic tasks, like reaching a pre-grasp configuration, are specified in the end effector space or task space, whereas, robot motion is controlled in joint space. Because of inherent actuation errors in joint space, robots cannot achieve desired configurations in task space exactly. Furthermore, different inverse kinematics (IK) solutions map joint space error set to task space differently. Thus for a given task with a prescribed error tolerance, all IK solutions will not be guaranteed to successfully execute the task. Any IK solution that is guaranteed to execute a task (possibly with high probability) irrespective of the realization of the joint space error is called a robust IK solution. In this paper we formulate and solve the robust inverse kinematics problem for redundant manipulators with actuation uncertainties (errors). We also present simulation and experimental results on a 7-DoF redundant manipulator for two applications, namely, a pre-grasp positioning and a pre-insertion positioning scenario. Our results show that the robust IK solutions result in higher success rates and also allows the robot to self-evaluate how successful it might be in any application scenario.

Abstract:
Manipulability analysis is a methodology employed to assess the capacity of an articulated system, at a specific configuration, to produce motion or exert force in diverse directions. The conventional method entails generating a virtual ellipsoid using the system’s configuration and model. Yet, this approach poses challenges when applied to systems such as the human body, where direct access to such information is limited, necessitating reliance on estimations. Any inaccuracies in these estimations can distort the ellipsoid’s configuration, potentially compromising the accuracy of the manipulability assessment. To address this issue, this article extends the standard approach by introducing the concept of the manipulability pseudo-ellipsoid. Through a series of theoretical analyses, simulations, and experiments, the article demonstrates that the proposed method exhibits reduced sensitivity to noise in sensory information, consequently enhancing the robustness of the approach.

Abstract:
Multi-robot teams can achieve more dexterous, complex and heavier payload tasks than a single robot, yet effective collaboration is required. Multi-robot collaboration is extremely challenging due to the different kinematic and dynamics capabilities of the robots, the limited communication between them, and the uncertainty of the system parameters. In this letter, a Decentralized Ability-Aware Adaptive Control (${DA}^3\!{C}$) is proposed to address these challenges based on two key features. Firstly, the common manipulation task is represented by the proposed nominal task ellipsoid, which is used to maximize each robot's force capability online via optimizing its configuration. Secondly, a decentralized adaptive controller is designed to be Lyapunov stable in spite of heterogeneous actuation constraints of the robots and uncertain physical parameters of the object and environment. In the proposed framework, decentralized coordination and load distribution between the robots is achieved without communication, while only the control deficiency is broadcast if any of the robots reaches its force limits. In this case, the object's reference trajectory is modified in a decentralized manner to guarantee stable interaction. Finally, we perform several numerical and physical simulations to analyse and verify the proposed method with heterogeneous multi-robot teams in collaborative manipulation tasks.

Abstract:

We present the Probabilistic-Product-Of-Exponentials robot model, a novel approach for kinematic modeling of robots. It does not only consider the robot's deterministic geometry but additionally models time-varying and configuration-dependent errors in a probabilistic way. Abstract:
<jats:p>The rapid development of digital manufacturing and robotic systems places increased demands on the accuracy and reliability of industrial manipulators. Traditional time-based reliability metrics do not reflect the robot’s ability to consistently achieve the desired position and orientation within process tolerances or the probability of the end-effector falling into a given area of permissible poses. The proposed framework integrates a deterministic kinematic model, a stochastic representation of Denavit–Hartenberg parameters and control variables, analytical methods for estimating probabilities, and numerical modeling using the Monte Carlo method. The methodology has been tested on the widely used industrial robot FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L. The results demonstrate a significant dependence of geometric reliability on the kinematic configuration of the manipulator, with maximum reliability in compact poses and a significant reduction in elongated configurations near singularities. Comprehensive validation was carried out, including numerical experiments on a planar prototype, high-precision physical measurements on a real robot and analysis of operational data, which confirmed the adequacy of the proposed model. The developed approach provides a powerful tool for designing, optimizing and predicting the reliability of robotic cells in high-precision automation environments.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Programs for one-armed industrial robots include many location-centric statements, such as "Move to location AboveSurface." Unfortunately, developers struggle to understand static location variables like AboveSurface, as mapping their seven-coordinate definitions to the real world is time consuming and error prone. Thus these locations, as well as the paths between them, which constitute the heart of any robot program, are effectively invisible to the programmer. To enable effective robot programming this core data must be visualized. There are two potential approaches to visualizing it. The first, visualizing locations one by one (e.g., by automatically moving the robot to each location) is limited to one location at a time. The second, visualizing locations in virtual reality can show all locations and paths at one time, but eliminates the ability to interact with the real world, which has many drawbacks. To avoid these drawbacks we propose using high-precision mixed reality to visualize program locations and paths, all while preserving the natural interaction with the real world workspace and robot. In this paper we demonstrate the feasibility of such an approach, sketch a solution, and discuss the advantages and disadvantages.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The purpose of our systematic review was to inspect the recently published research on Internet of Robotic Things (IoRT) and harmonize the assimilations it articulates on remote big data management tools, sensing and computing technologies, and visual perception and environment mapping algorithms. The research problems were whether robotic manufacturing processes and industrial wireless sensor networks shape IoRT and lead to improved product quality by use of remote big data management tools, whether IoRT devices communicate autonomously regarding event modeling and forecasting by leveraging machine learning and clustering algorithms, sensing and computing technologies, and image processing tools, and whether smart connected objects, situational awareness algorithms, and edge computing technologies configure IoRT systems and cloud robotics in relation to distributed task coordination through visual perception and environment mapping algorithms. A Shiny app was harnessed for Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) guidelines to configure the flow diagram integrating evidence-based gathered and processed data (the search outcomes and screening procedures). A quantitative literature review of ProQuest, Scopus, and the Web of Science databases was carried out throughout June and October 2022, with search terms including “Internet of Robotic Things” + “remote big data management tools”, “sensing and computing technologies”, and “visual perception and environment mapping algorithms”. Artificial intelligence and intelligent workflows by use of AMSTAR (Assessing the Methodological Quality of Systematic Reviews), Dedoose, DistillerSR, and SRDR (Systematic Review Data Repository) have been deployed as data extraction tools for literature collection, screening, and evaluation, for document flow monitoring, for inspecting qualitative and mixed methods research, and for establishing robust outcomes and correlations. For bibliometric mapping by use of data visualization, Dimensions AI was leveraged and with regards to layout algorithms, VOSviewer was harnessed.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Augmented reality (AR) is used to enhance the perception of the real world by integrating virtual objects to an image sequence acquired from various camera technologies. Numerous AR applications in robotics have been developed in recent years. The aim of this paper is to provide an overview of AR research in robotics during the five year period from 2015 to 2019. We classified these works in terms of application areas into four categories: (1) Medical robotics: Robot-Assisted surgery (RAS), prosthetics, rehabilitation, and training systems; (2) Motion planning and control: trajectory generation, robot programming, simulation, and manipulation; (3) Human-robot interaction (HRI): teleoperation, collaborative interfaces, wearable robots, haptic interfaces, brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), and gaming; (4) Multi-agent systems: use of visual feedback to remotely control drones, robot swarms, and robots with shared workspace. Recent developments in AR technology are discussed followed by the challenges met in AR due to issues of camera localization, environment mapping, and registration. We explore AR applications in terms of how AR was integrated and which improvements it introduced to corresponding fields of robotics. In addition, we summarize the major limitations of the presented applications in each category. Finally, we conclude our review with future directions of AR research in robotics. The survey covers over 100 research works published over the last five years.

Due to the specificity and complexity of hepatobiliary surgery, traditional preoperative imaging techniques such as computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging cannot meet the need for identification of fine anatomical regions. From text 'chen2015applicationofthe pages 14-18'.

KS Chen. Application of the iso 9283 standard to test repeatability of the baxter robot. Unknown journal, 2015.

The excerpt describes a measurement-based and robot-model-based approach for visualizing repeatability in three dimensions, but it does not identify specific visualization software or discuss error ellipsoids or error along a continuous path. Riemer and Edan measured target positions with a three-dimensional dial-gauge system, using 30 cycles per experiment and repeating each experiment 30 times. Repeatability was computed according to ISO 9283 from the average deviation of measured positions in 3D space and the standard deviation of that average deviation. For model-based visualization, inverse kinematics first determines the joint angles for each desired target location. Partial derivatives of the robot’s forward-kinematic model are then combined with measured joint-angle errors and robot angles. Cartesian error components are aggregated into a statistical error using the Euclidean form sqrt(Ex² + Ey² + Ez²), while an absolute error uses the corresponding component magnitudes. The experimentally validated statistical error model was used to generate a 3D map of repeatability over X-Y target positions at multiple heights. The map indicated that repeatability generally deteriorated as the target moved farther from the robot. The excerpt provides no method for constructing error ellipsoids, no path-based error calculation, and no named software package.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'chen2015applicationofthe pages 18-23'.

KS Chen. Application of the iso 9283 standard to test repeatability of the baxter robot. Unknown journal, 2015.

The excerpt describes measurement-based visualization and computation of robot repeatability, but it does not identify specific software packages, error ellipsoid methods, or error plotted along a continuous path. A 3D repeatability map can be generated by evaluating repeatability at target locations distributed across different X-Y positions and heights; the reported trend is that repeatability generally degrades farther from the robot. ISO 9283 provides a standardized sampling arrangement using a workspace test cube, a diagonal test plane, and five poses (P1–P5). Measurements are collected for 30 cycles while varying velocity (10%, 50%, and 100% of rated velocity) and payload (normally 100%, optionally 10%). Position repeatability is computed from the measured Cartesian points: calculate their barycentre (mean x, y, and z), determine each point’s Euclidean distance from that barycentre, calculate the mean and standard deviation of those distances, and report RPl = mean distance + three standard deviations. Orientation repeatability is computed separately for three rotation angles using three times the standard deviation of deviations from the mean angle. These statistics can supply scalar values for map visualization, although ellipsoid and path-error constructions are not specified in this excerpt.

This article has 35 citations.

The excerpt describes a probabilistic, Jacobian-based approach for visualizing robot positioning accuracy and repeatability in 3D. Robot parameter or drive-error uncertainties are represented by a covariance matrix Σq and propagated through the kinematic Jacobian, using the relationship ΣX = JqΣqJqT. The resulting Cartesian covariance can be visualized as 3D error ellipsoids, whose size and orientation reflect positioning uncertainty. Applying this calculation throughout sampled joint configurations or workspace points produces a geometric reliability or repeatability map: central, compact configurations generally show higher reliability, while peripheral regions show lower reliability because Jacobian coefficients and sensitivity to parameter errors increase. Reliability is defined probabilistically as R = P(X ∈ Ω), where Ω is the acceptable positioning tolerance region. For trajectory analysis, the same calculation is evaluated along θ(t), allowing reliability, variance, or error to be plotted against path position or time; trajectory planners can constrain R(θ(t)) to remain above a required threshold. The excerpt does not identify a dedicated visualization software package. It mentions compatibility with modern FANUC control systems and recommends using reliability maps for workspace screening, configuration selection, trajectory optimization, and recalibration triggering. The framework is also extensible to mobile, redundant, parallel, and collaborative robots when their kinematics and uncertainty models are available.

Abstract:
Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) offer great versatility for encoding, generating and adapting complex end-effector trajectories. DMPs are also very well suited to learning manipulation skills from human demonstration. However, the reactive nature of DMPs restricts their applicability for tool use and object manipulation tasks involving non-holonomic constraints, such as scalpel cutting or catheter steering. In this work, we extend the Cartesian space DMP formulation by adding a coupling term that enforces a pre-defined set of non-holonomic constraints. We obtain the closed-form expression for the constraint forcing term using the Udwadia-Kalaba method. This approach offers a clean and practical solution for guaranteed constraint satisfaction at run-time. Further, the proposed analytical form of the constraint forcing term enables efficient trajectory optimization subject to constraints. We demonstrate the usefulness of this approach by showing how we can learn robotic cutting skills from human demonstration.

Abstract:
Robot links are typically subjected to larger thermal deformations than machine-tool structures. In this study, the thermal effect on the two-dimensional (2D) positioning error of a planar robot arm over its entire workspace was investigated. It was experimentally verified that the Denavit–Hartenberg (DH) parameters, namely the link lengths and angular offset of the rotary axis, could be the key contributors to the thermal variation in the 2D positioning error. The experiment revealed that the variation in the angular positioning deviations of the rotary axes was marginal. This paper presents an on-machine test to identify the link lengths and the angular offset by probing an artifact bar of a pre-calibrated length. To compensate for the thermal influence, it is effective to identify the DH parameters by periodically performing the proposed test.

Abstract:
The advancement of simulation-assisted robot programming, automation of high-tolerance assembly operations, and improvement of real-world performance engender a need for positionally accurate robots. Despite tight machining tolerances, good mechanical design, and careful assembly, robotic arms typically exhibit average Cartesian positioning errors of several millimeters. Fortunately, the vast majority of this error can be removed in software by proper calibration of the so-called "zero-offsets" of a robot's joints. This research developed an automated, inexpensive, highly portable, in situ calibration method that fine tunes these kinematic parameters, thereby, improving a robot's average positioning accuracy four-fold throughout its workspace. In particular, a prospective low-cost motion capture system and a benchmark laser tracker were used as reference sensors for robot calibration. Bayesian inference produced optimized zero-offset parameters alongside their uncertainty for data from both reference sensors. Relative and absolute accuracy metrics were proposed and applied for quantifying robot positioning accuracy. Uncertainty analysis of a validated, probabilistic robot model quantified the absolute positioning accuracy throughout its entire workspace. Altogether, three measures of accuracy conclusively revealed multi-fold improvement in the positioning accuracy of the robotic arm. Bayesian inference on motion capture data yielded zero-offsets and accuracy calculations comparable to those derived from laser tracker data, ultimately proving this method's viability towards robot calibration.

Abstract:
The present study was carried out to investigate and analyze the positionning repeatability introduced by friction variations based on stochastic ellipsoids. A mixed friction model has been developed with improved properties compared to existing standard models. The contact is presented as a multitude of micro contacts whose nature can be of two types: lubricated and solid. This model is experimentally tested on a reciprocating tribometer under extreme friction conditions, with sliding speed varying from 0.1 to 3 m/s and load modified from 40N to 150N to discuss the effect of speed, the effect of nominal contact pressure and the effect of sliding distance on friction parameters. The results showed how this model can be represented as a sum of functions of the relevant states, which are linear and nonlinear in the friction parameters. Thus, these results were used to evaluate the covariance matrix in order to locate the different ranges of errors which have an impact on the repeatability of position.

## 7. Visual-Haptic Model Mediated Teleoperation for Remote Ultrasound

    year = "2025",

    volume = "abs/2502.07922",

    url = "https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2502.07922"

Abstract:
Tele-ultrasound has the potential greatly to improve health equity for countless remote communities. However, practical scenarios involve potentially large time delays which cause current implementations of telerobotic ultrasound (US) to fail. Using a local model of the remote environment to provide haptics to the expert operator can decrease teleoperation instability, but the delayed visual feedback remains problematic. This paper introduces a robotic tele-US system in which the local model is not only haptic, but also visual, by re-slicing and rendering a pre-acquired US sweep in real time to provide the operator a preview of what the delayed image will resemble. A prototype system is presented and tested with 15 volunteer operators. It is found that visual-haptic model-mediated teleoperation (MMT) compensates completely for time delays up to 1000 ms round trip in terms of operator effort and completion time while conventional MMT does not. Visual-haptic MMT also significantly outperforms MMT for longer time delays in terms of motion accuracy and force control. This proof-of-concept study suggests that visual-haptic MMT may facilitate remote robotic tele-US.

    author = "Saeidi, H. and Opfermann, J. and Kam, M. and Wei, Shuwen and Léonard, Simon and Hsieh, M. and Kang, Jin U. and Krieger, Axel",
    title = "Autonomous robotic laparoscopic surgery for intestinal anastomosis",

    publisher = "American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS)",
    issue = "62",

}


Abstract:
Autonomous robotic surgery has the potential to provide efficacy, safety, and consistency independent of individual surgeon’s skill and experience. Autonomous anastomosis is a challenging soft-tissue surgery task because it requires intricate imaging, tissue tracking, and surgical planning techniques, as well as a precise execution via highly adaptable control strategies often in unstructured and deformable environments. In the laparoscopic setting, such surgeries are even more challenging because of the need for high maneuverability and repeatability under motion and vision constraints. Here we describe an enhanced autonomous strategy for laparoscopic soft tissue surgery and demonstrate robotic laparoscopic small bowel anastomosis in phantom and in vivo intestinal tissues. This enhanced autonomous strategy allows the operator to select among autonomously generated surgical plans and the robot executes a wide range of tasks independently. We then use our enhanced autonomous strategy to perform in vivo autonomous robotic laparoscopic surgery for intestinal anastomosis on porcine models over a 1-week survival period. We compared the anastomosis quality criteria—including needle placement corrections, suture spacing, suture bite size, completion time, lumen patency, and leak pressure—of the developed autonomous system, manual laparoscopic surgery, and robot-assisted surgery (RAS). Data from a phantom model indicate that our system outperforms expert surgeons’ manual technique and RAS technique in terms of consistency and accuracy. This was also replicated in the in vivo model. These results demonstrate that surgical robots exhibiting high levels of autonomy have the potential to improve consistency, patient outcomes, and access to a standard surgical technique. Description An autonomous robotic strategy allows laparoscopic soft tissue surgery in end-to-end anastomosis of the small bowel.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Ultrasound (US) imaging is a widely used diagnostic method in clinics. Real-time-generated US images are used for rapid diagnosis without harm to patients. The quality of US imaging highly depends on the skill of the physician due to the differences among physicians. Techniques for autonomous robotic ultrasound (AU-RUS) acquisitions are expected to become an effective means to improve the level of US diagnosis, reduce the workload of physicians, and improve the standardization of US imaging quality. This paper aims to summarize the current research status of techniques for AU-RUS acquisitions, and to discuss the research trends and challenges regarding related technologies. Firstly, the techniques for AU-RUS acquisitions and systems are outlined. The techniques for teleoperated or autonomous US acquisitions are briefly discussed. Representative RUS acquisition systems are introduced. Then, the current research status of AU-RUS acquisitions is reviewed from four research directions: force sensitivity and control, scanning path-planning and positioning, US treatment guidance, and US image processing technology and quality assessment optimization. This review provides a decision-oriented autonomy perspective by mapping typical methods to workflow components across the stages of perception, decision-making, and execution. We identify major deployment bottlenecks, including safety-verifiable autonomy and failure recovery, motion compensation under deformation, and the lack of standardized, clinically meaningful US image quality metrics. Finally, the shortcomings of current research are summarized and analyzed, and the research trends and challenges for AU-RUS acquisitions are prospected.</jats:p>

From text 'makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 5-7'.

Kaldybek Makhambetov, Nadezhda Kunicina, Antons Patlins, Gulshat Amirkhanova, Baurzhan Belgibayev, and Saltanat Adilzhanova. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095, doi:10.3390/electronics15143095. This article has 0 citations.

The stochastic ellipsoid method represents robot positioning or repeatability uncertainty at each nominal configuration using the covariance of Monte Carlo end-effector errors. For every sampled joint configuration, the nominal position is computed, random joint and geometric perturbations are generated from the specified noise models, and each perturbed position is propagated through forward kinematics. The displacement samples are calculated as Δp = p_noisy − p_nom, then their covariance matrix Σ is eigendecomposed as Σ = VDVᵀ. The eigenvectors in V define the principal directions of the uncertainty ellipsoid, while the eigenvalues λj represent variances along those directions. A 3σ ellipsoid uses semi-axis lengths aj = 3√λj; its volume, (4/3)π∏aj, summarizes total three-dimensional uncertainty while retaining directional information that scalar RMS omits. Monte Carlo workspace maps repeat this process across many configurations. The excerpt describes 50 configurations with 10,000 noise trials each for detailed analysis, and a separate workspace probability map using 3,000 uniformly sampled configurations within joint limits and 500 trials per point, totaling 1,500,000 forward-kinematics evaluations. RMS and P95 errors provide scalar accuracy measures, while ellipsoid parameters and spatial aggregation characterize probabilistic accuracy throughout the reachable workspace.

The excerpt describes a stochastic ellipsoid and workspace-mapping procedure for robot positioning uncertainty. For a selected robot configuration, the position-error covariance matrix is decomposed into eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The eigenvectors define the principal directions of uncertainty, while the eigenvalues determine the ellipsoid semi-axis lengths; the displayed 3σ ellipsoid represents the corresponding uncertainty region and approximately 99.7% of realizations under the assumed distribution. Repeatability can therefore be characterized probabilistically by the ellipsoid’s orientation, axes, and volume, supplemented by sampled error vectors and RMS error. For probabilistic workspace maps, the method randomly samples thousands of end-effector or workspace configurations. At each configuration, Monte Carlo trials propagate modeled noise and uncertainty through the manipulator, producing position-error realizations, covariance estimates, RMS errors, and related statistics. The resulting Cartesian locations are rendered as a colored point cloud: green denotes RMS error below 5 mm, yellow 5–15 mm, and red above 15 mm. The excerpt reports 3000 workspace points with 500 Monte Carlo trials for visualization, while broader stochastic analysis uses 10,000 trials across 50 configurations. In the conventional covariance-based construction, the ellipsoid is centered at the nominal end-effector position and its principal directions are the eigenvectors of the Cartesian position covariance matrix; the semi-axis lengths are proportional to the square roots of the corresponding eigenvalues, with the multiplier set to the desired confidence level (such as 3σ). The reported ellipsoids are anisotropic: their longest axis is primarily vertical, consistent with gravity-induced elastic deformation. Their volumes and aspect ratios vary by workspace region, providing repeatability and tolerance information. The stochastic ellipsoid method therefore captures not only overall variance but also directional and configuration-dependent uncertainty. For probabilistic workspace maps, the study samples 3,000 robot configurations and performs 500 Monte Carlo trials per configuration, totaling 1,500,000 evaluations. The excerpt describes a stochastic error-ellipsoid approach for robot positioning and repeatability. Positioning uncertainty is represented as a spatial distribution of end-effector errors; its covariance determines the ellipsoid’s principal directions and spread. The ellipsoid axes align with directions of greatest variability, which are associated with large sensitivities in the Jacobian (Jacobi) matrix. Nearly spherical ellipsoids indicate similar sensitivity in all directions, while elongated or inclined ellipsoids indicate anisotropic uncertainty and correlated link or drive errors. The study compares compact, medium, and elongated robot configurations. For the FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L, measurements used 25 workspace points and 50 repeated trials per point, with a laser tracker accurate to about 0.01 mm. These repeated samples were used to construct empirical error distributions and covariance matrices, which were compared against model predictions. Monte Carlo analysis was especially important in highly nonlinear or elongated configurations, where analytical and stochastic estimates differed by 7–10%; compact and medium configurations differed by only 1–3%. Thus, probabilistic workspace mapping involves sampling model uncertainties across configurations, estimating covariance/error ellipsoids at workspace locations, and using the resulting map to identify sensitive regions and optimize configurations before assembly or during online condition assessment.

The excerpt describes the covariance-based foundation for stochastic robot positioning. Kinematic and joint errors are modeled as random variables, typically with a multivariate normal distribution q ~ N(μq, Σq), where Σq can include correlations between parameters. Forward kinematics is linearized around the nominal or mean parameter vector: δX ≈ Jqδq. The end-effector pose covariance is then computed by propagating parameter covariance through the kinematic Jacobian: ΣX = JqΣqJqᵀ. An error ellipsoid for position is obtained from the relevant 3×3 translational block of ΣX: its principal axes and directions come from eigenvectors and eigenvalues, while a selected confidence level scales the semi-axis lengths by the corresponding chi-square quantile. For full pose uncertainty, a six-dimensional covariance can similarly describe position and orientation jointly, though orientation requires suitable angular treatment. A stochastic ellipsoid repeatability method therefore samples or propagates uncertain parameters, computes the resulting pose covariance, and represents repeatability with confidence ellipsoids. The excerpt does not describe a Monte Carlo workspace-map algorithm explicitly. However, Monte Carlo mapping would repeatedly draw q from N(μq, Σq), evaluate forward kinematics X = f(q) at workspace configurations, and aggregate empirical means, covariances, confidence ellipsoids, failure probabilities, or dispersion values into a spatial probabilistic/error map. High Jacobian conditioning and singular configurations produce larger mapped uncertainties.

Abstract:
To increase the reliability of collaborative robots in performing daily tasks, we require them to be accurate and not only repeatable. However, having a calibrated kinematics model is regrettably a luxury, as available calibration tools are usually more expensive than the robots themselves. With this work, we aim to contribute to the democratization of cobots calibration by providing an inexpensive yet highly effective alternative to existing tools. The proposed minimalist calibration routine relies on a 3D-printable tool as the only physical aid to the calibration process. This two-socket spherical-joint tool kinematically constrains the robot at the end effector while collecting the training set. An optimization routine updates the nominal model to ensure a consistent prediction for each socket and the undistorted mean distance between them. We validated the algorithm on three robotic platforms: Franka, Kuka, and Kinova Cobots. The calibrated models reduce the mean absolute error from the order of 10 mm to 0.2 mm for both Franka and Kuka robots. We provide two additional experimental campaigns with the Franka Robot to render the improvements more tangible. First, we implement Cartesian control with and without the calibrated model and use it to perform a standard peg-in-the-hole task with a tolerance of 0.4 mm between the peg and the hole. Second, we perform a repeated drawing task combining Cartesian control with learning from demonstration. Both tasks consistently failed when the model was not calibrated, while they consistently succeeded after calibration.
