ISO 9283 provides 14 robot-performance tests. Testing is conducted at maximum possible payload and speed, using an imaginary ISO cube positioned in the robot workspace. A selected diagonal and measurement points are used; the example selects five points, P1–P5, and the position-accuracy protocol requires 100% payload, 100% speed, five measuring points, and 30 cycles. Position accuracy (AP) is the deviation between the commanded position and the mean achieved position. The excerpt identifies unidirectional position repeatability (RP), path repeatability (RT), distance accuracy (AD), and distance repeatability (RD) as related criteria, although complete repeatability-specific trial conditions are not shown. ISO 9283 does not prescribe a particular metrology system. Reported tools and results include a laser tracker, laser interferometer, and Renishaw ballbar used on an ABB IRB 1600: repeatability was 22–37 mm with the laser tracker, 6–14 mm with the laser interferometer, and circularity deviation was below 1 mm with the ballbar. Other tested arms include a Yaskawa Motoman HP20F, whose repeatability worsened with increasing cycles and was several hundredths of a millimeter worse than its stated RP = 0.06 mm, and an ABB IRB 1200 5/0.9, whose thermal-drift repeatability improved from about 200 µm to 25 µm after compensation. The excerpt provides the clearest ISO 9283 protocol for the CRS A255 experiment, but it does not reproduce the full standard’s positioning-accuracy procedure or a separate accuracy success threshold. Abstract:
<jats:p>Upper-limb motor impairment is a major consequence of stroke and neuromuscular disorders, imposing a sustained clinical and socioeconomic burden worldwide. Quantitative assessment of limb positioning and motion accuracy is fundamental to rehabilitation, guiding therapy evaluation and robotic assistance. The evolution of upper-limb positioning systems has progressed from optical motion capture to wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) and, more recently, to data-driven estimators integrated with rehabilitation robots. Each generation has aimed to balance spatial accuracy, portability, latency, and metrological reliability under ecological conditions. This review presents a systematic synthesis of the state of measurement uncertainty, calibration, and traceability in upper-limb rehabilitation robotics. Studies are categorised across four layers, i.e., sensing, fusion, cognitive, and metrological, according to their role in data acquisition, estimation, adaptation, and verification. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) protocol was followed to ensure transparent identification, screening, and inclusion of relevant works. Comparative evaluation highlights how modern sensor-fusion and learning-based pipelines achieve near-optical angular accuracy while maintaining clinical usability. Persistent challenges include non-standard calibration procedures, magnetometer vulnerability, limited uncertainty propagation, and absence of unified traceability frameworks. The synthesis indicates a gradual transition toward cognitive and uncertainty-aware rehabilitation robotics in which metrology, artificial intelligence, and control co-evolve. Traceable measurement chains, explainable estimators, and energy-efficient embedded deployment emerge as essential prerequisites for regulatory and clinical translation. The review concludes that future upper-limb systems must integrate calibration transparency, quantified uncertainty, and interpretable learning to enable reproducible, patient-centred rehabilitation by 2030.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Pose estimation problems are fundamental in robotics. Most of these problems are challenging due to the nonconvex nature. This also sets up an obstacle for uncertainty description that is essential for pose integration and quality control. In this article, we show that a large class of related problems can be categorized as the quadratic pose estimation problems (QPEPs) and we propose a general quaternion-based mathematical model to unify these problems. To solve the nonconvex QPEPs, a Gröbner-basis method is investigated to derive their globally optimal and robust solutions. Furthermore, we develop the rules for characterizing the solvability and observability of these solutions. In addition, the uncertainty description, i.e., covariance matrix, as an important piece of information in robotic state estimation frameworks, is analyzed in detail. Theoretical results show that the covariance can be estimated via online optimization, in an efficient and unbiased manner. In this way, both the solution and covariance are guaranteed to be globally optimal. Through simulations and experiments, we show that the proposed QPEP-based solver is not only accurate, robust, and efficient but outperforms the representatives for covariance estimation. The designed algorithms are also assembled as a C++/MATLAB/Octave/ROS library, while these developed interfaces are built for main stream platforms and simultaneous localization and mapping schemes.

Abstract:
Conventional industrial robots are increasingly used for milling applications of large workpieces due to their workspace and their low investment costs in comparison to conventional machine tools. However, static deflections and dynamic instabilities during the milling process limit the efficiency and productivity of such robot-based milling systems. Since the pose-dependent dynamic properties of the industrial robot structures are notoriously difficult to model analytically, machine learning methods are recently gaining more and more popularity to derive system models from experimental data. In this publication, a modeling concept based on a modern information fusion scheme, fusing simulation and experimental data, is proposed. This approach provides a precise model of the robot’s pose-dependent structural dynamics and is validated for a one-dimensional variation of the robot pose. The results of two information fusion algorithms are compared with a conventional, data-driven approach and indicate a superior model accuracy regarding interpolation and extrapolation of the pose-dependent dynamics. The proposed approach enables decreasing the necessary amount of experimental data needed to assess the vibrational properties of the robot for a desired pose. Additionally, the concept is able to predict the robot dynamics at poses where experimental data is very costly to gather.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The autonomous flight capability of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in complex dynamic environments highly depends on the accurate perception of the environment and their own state by onboard sensors. However, limited by sensor noise, model mismatch, observation heterogeneity, and external environmental disturbances, the output of onboard sensors inherently possesses significant uncertainty and randomness. How to transform imperfect, multi-source, and asynchronous sensor observations into reliable state estimation and environmental cognition results through statistical modeling and inference methods has become one of the core issues in UAV perception system research. This paper systematically reviews the development of research related to UAV onboard sensors from a statistical perspective, focusing on the application and evolution of statistical modeling, state estimation, and multi-sensor fusion methods in UAV perception systems. First, it summarizes the typical statistical observation models and noise characteristics of inertial sensors, satellite navigation, vision, lidar, and novel neuromorphic sensors, and analyzes key statistical issues such as random walk, non-Gaussian noise, and time-dependent errors. Subsequently, based on the Bayesian state estimation framework, this paper systematically reviews the application progress of Kalman filtering, error state filtering, particle filtering, and robust statistical methods in UAV navigation and localization, and compares and analyzes the statistical nature of loosely coupled and tightly coupled multi-sensor fusion strategies. Building upon this, it further discusses joint probabilistic modeling methods for heterogeneous sensors such as vision, inertial, and radar, as well as the fusion trend of statistical learning and deep models in high-dimensional perception tasks. Finally, this paper summarizes the role and limitations of statistical methods in UAV airborne sensor research and looks forward to future development directions oriented towards uncertainty perception (the capability to explicitly quantify the reliability of perception results), risk-constrained decision-making (strategies that incorporate estimation variance into control loops to ensure operational safety), and integrated sensing-computing architectures.</jats:p>

                           Abstract

                            Physical access to robotic manipulators remains constrained by cost, safety requirements,
                       and limited laboratory availability, creating barriers to both research and education.
                           This paper presents a computational framework that combines stochastic error model-
                           ing with Digital Twin technology to characterize positioning uncertainty in a six-degree-
                          of-freedom manipulator without requiring physical hardware. Four independent noise
                           sources—joint encoder noise, thermal drift, elastic link deformation, and geometric param-
                                eter tolerances—are modeled as stochastic processes and propagated through the manipu-
                                lator kinematics using Monte Carlo simulation with N = 10,000 trials across 50 workspace
                             configurations. The results reveal that elastic deformation dominates the combined po-
                              sitioning error by a factor of 45.94 over encoder noise, contributing 99.97% of the total
                          root-mean-square (RMS) uncertainty. A probabilistic workspace map constructed from
                          3000 sampled configurations quantifies accuracy and manipulability across the reachable

                             1. Introduction

                           The deployment of robotic manipulators across manufacturing, medical, and educa-
                              tional settings has accelerated considerably over the past decade, driven by advances in
                            mechatronics, embedded computing, and control theory [1,2]. Despite this growth, the gap
                         between theoretical control design and physical implementation remains wide. Laborato-
                                  ries capable of hosting industrial-grade manipulators are expensive to equip and maintain,
                        and the operational risks associated with unvalidated control algorithms—collision, actua-
                                tor damage, injury—discourage experimental iteration [3]. These constraints are especially
                            acute in academic environments, where student-to-robot ratios are unfavorable and super-
                            vised access hours are limited.
                                   Digital Twin technology has emerged as a principled response to this problem. By
                          maintaining a continuously updated virtual replica of a physical system, a Digital Twin
                           enables simulation, monitoring, and predictive analysis without direct hardware interac-
                              tion [4,5]. This framework acts as an intelligent manufacturing system component within
                        an Industrial IoT (IIoT) infrastructure, where the cyber–physical integration of real-time
                    ROS messaging and virtual replica environments defines the smart space. The proposed
                               Digital Twin architecture aligns with the IoT-Enabled Smart Devices and Systems paradigm
                       by providing bidirectional data flow between the physical manipulator and its virtual
                             counterpart, enabling real-time monitoring, stochastic performance prediction, and control
                             validation within a smart manufacturing environment [4,5].
                                 In robotics, Digital Twins have been applied to trajectory planning, fault detection,
                       and operator training, with recent work demonstrating that high-fidelity kinematic and
                        dynamic models can reproduce physical robot behavior with sub-millimeter accuracy [6,7].
                      What remains less explored is the integration of stochastic uncertainty models within the
                              Digital Twin framework—that is, using the virtual replica not merely to replicate nominal
                             behavior, but to characterize the probabilistic envelope of positioning errors arising from
                            real-world noise sources.
                                  Positioning accuracy in robotic manipulators is affected by multiple concurrent uncer-
                               tainty sources. Joint encoder quantization and noise introduce angular measurement errors
                              that propagate nonlinearly through the forward kinematics [8]. Manufacturing tolerances
                       on link dimensions and joint axis orientations produce systematic geometric offsets that
                               persist across all configurations [9]. Thermal expansion of structural components during
                           sustained operation shifts the effective Denavit–Hartenberg parameters away from their
                              calibrated values [10]. Perhaps most significantly, elastic deformation of links under gravi-
                                tational and inertial loading introduces configuration-dependent deflections that can reach
                              tens of millimeters in extended poses [11,12]. These sources have been studied individually
                               in the literature, but their combined stochastic effect

                                 This apparently paradoxical result has a straightforward mechanical explanation. The
                            manipulability index reaches its maximum when the Jacobian is well-conditioned, which
                            occurs in configurations where the arm is extended away from singular postures. These ex-
                          tended configurations simultaneously maximize the gravitational moment arm on the distal
                                 links, producing larger elastic deflections and therefore larger positioning errors. The color
                          coding confirms this interpretation: elevated positions (yellow-green points, Z = 40–80 cm)
                               cluster at higher manipulability values and higher error values simultaneously.
                            The weakness of the correlation (r2 = 0.030, indicating that manipulability explains only
                         3.0% of error variance) underscores that the manipulability index, despite its widespread
                          use as a configuration quality measure, is an unreliable predictor of stochastic position-
                           ing accuracy. This finding motivates the full probabilistic workspace map developed in
                             Section 3.4 as a more informative planning tool.

                     SMC achieved a mean steady-state error of 0.0029 mm, a 48.2% reduction relative
                              to RPBCL (0.0056 mm). The improvement is consistent across all reported metrics: RMS
                              error decreased by 49.2%, standard deviation by 64.9%, and P95 by 64.9%. The boxplot in
                            Figure 8b shows that SMC’s interquartile range is approximately half that of RPBCL, and
                              that RPBCL produces four outliers above 11 × 10−3 mm while SMC produces only one
                         above 7.5 × 10−3 mm. The empirical CDF in Figure 8c makes the practical significance clear:
                               at a tolerance threshold of 5 µm, SMC achieves 99% compliance while RPBCL achieves
                           only 50%.
                                 In addition to steady-state accuracy, dynamic performance metrics were extracted
                        from the convergence trajectories over 200 Monte Carlo trials. SMC achieves a mean rise
                          time of 0.18 ± 0.02 s (42% faster than RPBCL: 0.31 ± 0.04 s) and a mean settling time of
                               0.97 ± 0.14 s (32% shorter than RPBCL: 1.42 ± 0.21 s). Neither controller exhibits overshoot
                         under the applied saturation mechanisms (tanh for RPBCL, boundary layer approximation
                                for SMC). These results confirm that SMC outperforms RPBCL across all evaluated metrics:
                              steady-state accuracy, convergence speed, and settling time.
                            The superior performance of SMC is attributable to the invariance property of sliding
                     mode dynamics. Once the system reaches the sliding surface s = 0, bounded disturbances
                              satisfying ∥d∥< η are rejected without affecting the sliding behavior. The boundary
                              layer saturation function F(s) prevents chattering while preserving this rejection property,
                              resulting in more consistent final positioning across noise realizations. RPBCL, which
                             applies a smooth gradient correction proportional to the error, has no analogous rejection
                       mechanism and accumulates the effect of each noise realization independently.

                             4. Discussion

                           The results presented in this work carry several implications that extend beyond the
                                specific manipulator configuration studied.
                             Regarding uncertainty sources, the overwhelming dominance of elastic deforma-
                              tion (97% of combined error) challenges the conventional focus on encoder precision in
                          manipulator design.
                            While modern encoders achieve resolutions below 0.001 rad, the present analysis
                           demonstrates that such improvements yield negligible accuracy gains when link compliance
                          remains uncompensated. This finding is consistent with the stiffness identification work
                              of Alici and Shirinzadeh [11] and Dumas et al. [12], who independently identified elastic
                              deflection as the primary accuracy limitation in serial manipulators under gravitational
                             loading. The implication for engineering practice is direct: accuracy improvement budgets

## pqac-00000039

From text 'issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 45-48'.

Madina Issametova, Nikita V. Martyushev, Boris V. Malozyomov, Anton Y. Demin, Alexander V. Pogrebnoy, Elizaveta E. Kuleshova, and Denis V. Valuev. Reliability in robotics and intelligent systems: mathematical modeling and algorithmic innovations. Mathematics, 14:580, Feb 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/math14030580, doi:10.3390/math14030580. This article has 35 citations.

The excerpt reports results only for the FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L; it provides no information about Kinova, UR5, Franka, ABB, or other low-cost robot arms. For the FANUC arm, analytical and Monte Carlo models agreed closely in compact and medium configurations, where errors were approximately normal and covariance estimates matched direct linearization. In the elongated configuration, nonlinear kinematic effects caused asymmetric and shifted error distributions. Experimental error ellipsoids showed that the major axis could be displaced by up to 10–11° relative to model predictions, with variance up to 20% higher than predicted. The study also constructed a workspace geometric-reliability map representing successful positioning probability. Reliability was approximately 0.98 in central workspace regions associated with compact configurations and declined toward the workspace boundaries, reaching low values around 0.70 in peripheral zones. The excerpt additionally reports that positioning accuracy degraded over time: average position error increased from 0.018 mm in the first three months to 0.041 mm in the last three months, while average orientation error rose from 0.28° to 0.71°. Thus, the provided passage supports detailed conclusions for FANUC only, not comparative results for the other named robot families.


---

## pqac-00000040

From text 'issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 28-29'.

Madina Issametova, Nikita V. Martyushev, Boris V. Malozyomov, Anton Y. Demin, Alexander V. Pogrebnoy, Elizaveta E. Kuleshova, and Denis V. Valuev. Reliability in robotics and intelligent systems: mathematical modeling and algorithmic innovations. Mathematics, 14:580, Feb 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/math14030580, doi:10.3390/math14030580. This article has 35 citations.

The excerpt reports probabilistic positioning and reliability analysis only for the six-axis FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L; it does not mention Kinova, UR5, Franka, ABB, or low-cost robot arms, nor does it provide comparative results for those models using error ellipsoids or workspace-accuracy maps. For FANUC, Monte Carlo simulations incorporated stochastic DH-parameter and joint errors, nonlinear direct kinematics, complex permissible regions, correlated errors, and dependence on configuration and trajectory. The analysis produced a reliability map over joint-configuration space, allowing identification of more reliable postures and avoidance of singularity-prone regions. Independent errors in joints 4–6 were associated primarily with orientation errors, while correlated errors in joints 1–3 caused vertical or horizontal displacement of the working point. Correlated errors in DH parameters altered the spatial distribution of posture errors. The robot’s outstretched-arm configurations, particularly those with a large second-joint angle, showed significantly reduced reliability because of increased Jacobian sensitivity. The excerpt also notes that the robot has low independent drive errors, although thermal expansion can produce correlated errors. Monte Carlo was considered useful for complex configuration-dependent reliability assessment, despite high computational cost and the need for importance sampling in rare-event, low-reliability cases.

## pqac-00000041

From text 'franzese2025mukcaaccurateand pages 4-6'.

Giovanni Franzese, Max Spahn, Jens Kober, and C. D. Santina. Mukca: accurate and affordable cobot calibration without external measurement devices. ArXiv, Mar 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2503.12584, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2503.12584. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt does not report tests using error ellipsoids, workspace accuracy maps, or probabilistic positioning analyses. It describes MUKCa calibration experiments on four Franka 7-DoF robots (three Panda models and one FR3), one KUKA iiwa 14, and two Kinova Gen3Lite arms. Franka results were strongest: test-set mean absolute error was reduced to 0.347 mm for Panda (1), 0.238 mm for Panda (2), 0.262 mm for Panda (3), and 0.278 mm for FR3, corresponding to approximately 92.69–97.53% error removal. KUKA’s error decreased to 0.268 mm on the test set, while the text specifically states a final error of 0.107 mm, matching repeatability. Kinova improved less substantially: test-set error decreased from 5.99 mm to 2.66 mm, removing 52.08% of the error; the authors attribute the limitation to joint backlash in planetary gearboxes and report an average calibrated error of about 2 mm from an initial 5 mm. No results for FANUC, UR5, ABB, or other unspecified low-cost arms appear in this excerpt. The cited figures show training curves, not ellipsoid or probabilistic positioning analyses.

The probabilistic robot kinematics model and its application to sensor fusion. 2022 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), pages 3263-3270, Oct 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/iros47612.2022.9981399, doi:10.1109/iros47612.2022.9981399. This article has 12 citations.

The excerpt reports experiments involving two robot platforms. First, it evaluates a simulated David humanoid robot, using fingertip contact with a simulated table to study residual end-effector pose errors. The PPOE covariance model encodes correlations between positional state variables and improves translational pose estimation; rotational error is largely unaffected. Second, it evaluates a planetary rover prototype (LRU) equipped with a Kinova Jaco2 arm. The arm’s end-effector pose is corrected by fusing 2D AprilTag image measurements with the 6D kinematic pose. The study models uncertainty from a flexing carbon-fiber base plate, joint errors, and hand-eye calibration residuals. In two experiments, PPOE-based 2D estimation achieved mean lateral errors of 0.29 ± 0.15 cm and 0.50 ± 0.25 cm, compared with 0.44 ± 0.29 cm and 0.52 ± 0.24 cm for a static naive covariance; forward kinematics alone produced 0.82 ± 0.49 cm and 1.48 ± 0.38 cm. The excerpt contains no tests or results for FANUC, UR5, Franka, ABB, or unspecified low-cost robot arms, and it does not describe workspace accuracy maps or error-ellipsoid evaluations for those models.

The excerpt reports probabilistic positioning analysis for a two-link planar prototype and relates its error behavior to the real FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L six-axis manipulator. For the prototype, 100,000 Monte Carlo realizations produced an elongated elliptical endpoint distribution. The permissible workspace region was circular with a 0.7 mm radius. Analytical reliability, based on a bivariate normal approximation and chi-square calculation, was 0.936, while Monte Carlo reliability was 0.939. Average position deviations were 0.52 mm analytically and 0.53 mm by Monte Carlo; the ellipse major-axis values were 0.94 and 0.96 mm, respectively. The difference between the methods was below 0.3%. Comparisons across three robot configurations showed discrepancies below 1.2% for compact and medium configurations, but 2.1% for an elongated configuration near kinematic singularities. Extended configurations generated greater endpoint dispersion and lower reliability. The excerpt does not provide results for Kinova, UR5, Franka, ABB, or unspecified low-cost robot arms, nor does it describe workspace accuracy maps by those manufacturers. It only establishes the prototype results and the corresponding FANUC comparison/framework.

| **Error ellipsoids (stochastic ellipsoid method)** | A 3D confidence region around the nominal or mean TCP position. Orientation shows principal error directions, semi-axis lengths show directional dispersion, and volume summarizes overall uncertainty. | From measured or simulated Cartesian errors, compute covariance Σ and eigendecompose it as Σ = VDVᵀ. Eigenvectors give principal directions and eigenvalues λ_j give variances. A 3σ ellipsoid has semi-axes a_j = 3√λ_j. Joint-space uncertainty can also be propagated into task space through the Jacobian. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000030) | **Measured:** command the same pose repeatedly, record 3D TCP coordinates, subtract their mean, and estimate Σ. Issametova et al. tested a FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L at 25 workspace points with 50 trials per point using a laser tracker accurate to about 0.01 mm. **Modeled:** Makhambetov et al. used 10,000 Monte Carlo trials at each of 50 configurations; that study was simulation-only and deferred physical validation. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000019) | NumPy/SciPy or MATLAB for covariance and eigendecomposition; Matplotlib, Plotly, Open3D, or Unity3D for rendering. The cited digital twin used MATLAB and Unity3D. | Makhambetov et al. (2026), [DOI 10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095); Issametova et al. Display measured samples directly or interpolate them only when spatial sampling is sufficiently dense. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014) | Makhambetov et al. sampled **3,000 configurations with 500 trials each**, totaling 1.5 million forward-kinematics evaluations. Points were green below 5 mm RMS, yellow from 5–15 mm, and red above 15 mm. messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Tool/Library | Language | Key Capabilities for Accuracy Visualization | Published Reference | Availability/Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **pytransform3d** | Python | Represents uncertain SE(3) transforms with 6×6 covariance; composes globally and locally uncertain transforms with `concat_globally_uncertain_transforms` and `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms`; changes covariance frames with `adjoint_from_transform`; projects 6D confidence hyperellipsoids into 3D; supports trajectory covariance, URDF kinematics, Matplotlib, and Open3D. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000044) | Fabisch & Popescu, *Frontiers in Robotics and AI* (2026), [doi:10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457) | Open-source Python library. Particularly suitable for an inexpensive, scriptable pipeline from URDF and measured covariance to ellipsoids along a trajectory. |
| **MATLAB + Unity3D Digital Twin** | MATLAB; C#/Unity | MATLAB performs Monte Carlo propagation, covariance/eigendecomposition, RMS and P95 calculations, and workspace sampling; Unity3D interactively renders color-coded probabilistic workspace point clouds, 3D error ellipsoids, and controller diagnostics. The published example used 10,000 trials at 50 configurations and a map of 3,000 configurations with 500 trials each. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000036) | Makhambetov et al., *Electronics* (2026), [doi:10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095) | MATLAB and Unity are separate products; Unity has free-use tiers, while MATLAB generally requires a license. The cited manipulator analysis is simulation-only, so its maps should not be treated as measured arm performance. |
| **RoboDK** | Python API; proprietary application | Robot simulation and offline programming; defines an ISO test cube and measurement plane, teaches targets on surfaces, generates point-visit programs, checks reachability, and visualizes nominal paths. Pollák and Goryl used it to prepare five ISO-style targets and separate X/Y measurement programs. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) | Pollák & Goryl, *Machines* (2023), [doi:10.3390/machines11070734](https://doi.org/10.3390/machines11070734) | Commercial software with educational/trial options. The cited evidence does **not** establish a built-in statistical repeatability-map or covariance-ellipsoid facility; export measurements to Python or MATLAB for those analyses. |
| **Probabilistic Product-of-Exponentials (PPOE)** | Mathematical model; research implementations commonly in C++/Python/MATLAB | Lie-group-based probabilistic kinematics that represents correlated, configuration-dependent errors and propagates them along a kinematic chain to a 6-DoF end-effector covariance. Demonstrated on a Kinova Jaco2 with AprilTag observations and VICON ground truth; suitable for configuration-dependent covariance or projected confidence-volume displays. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000042) | Meyer, Strobl & Triebel, IROS (2022), [doi:10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399](https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399) | A modeling method rather than a turnkey visualization application. A practical implementation path is PPOE covariance propagation followed by pytransform3d, Open3D, or RViz rendering. |
| **ROS / RViz** | C++; Python; ROS messages | ROS `tf`/`tf2` maintains frame relationships; RViz displays robot models, measured and commanded paths, point clouds, arrows, and custom marker or triangle meshes that can encode ellipsoids. It can serve as the live display layer for AprilTag-derived TCP samples and path-error overlays. pytransform3d’s `TransformManager` is explicitly inspired by ROS `tf`. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) | No dedicated peer-reviewed accuracy-map implementation was established in the retrieved evidence; related transformation and uncertainty functionality is documented by Fabisch & Popescu (2026), [doi:10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457](https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457) | Open source and well suited to live experiments. Ellipsoid fitting, confidence scaling, and repeatability statistics must be calculated in a separate node; RViz primarily renders the resulting markers. |
| **MATLAB Robotics Toolbox / NumPy + SciPy** | MATLAB or Python | General-purpose implementation route for forward kinematics, Jacobians, covariance estimation, eigendecomposition, Monte Carlo sampling, RMS/P95 statistics, interpolation, and ellipsoid meshes. The core operations are Σₓ = JΣqJᵀ and Σ = VDVᵀ, with confidence semi-axes derived from √λ. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000030) | The retrieved literature supports the underlying workflow in Makhambetov et al. (2026), [doi:10.3390/electronics15143095](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15143095), and Issametova et al. (2026), [doi:10.3390/math14030580](https://doi.org/10.3390/math14030580) | NumPy/SciPy are open source; MATLAB and some toolboxes require licenses. No retrieved paper establishes a one-click repeatability-map function in either stack—the analysis must be assembled from their numerical and plotting primitives. |

{"answer": "# Visualizing Robot Positioning Accuracy and Repeatability in 3D

## 1. Overview

Three principal methods appear in the published literature for showing a robot's positioning accuracy and repeatability in three dimensions: **(1) error ellipsoids** (the stochastic ellipsoid method), **(2) probabilistic workspace maps**, and **(3) Jacobian-based confidence volumes along a path or trajectory**. Each can be computed from physical measurements, from modeled parameter uncertainties, or from both. The table below summarizes these methods, their mathematical basis, published protocols, and supporting software.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## 2. Error Ellipsoids (Stochastic Ellipsoid Method)

### 2.1 Mathematical Construction

The stochastic ellipsoid method represents positioning uncertainty at a given robot configuration as a three-dimensional confidence region derived from the covariance of end-effector position errors. Makhambetov et al. describe the procedure: "The displacement samples are calculated as Δp = p_noisy − p_nom, then their covariance matrix Σ is eigendecomposed as Σ = VDVᵀ. The eigenvectors in V define the principal directions of the uncertainty ellipsoid, while the eigenvalues λ_j represent variances along those directions. A 3σ ellipsoid uses semi-axis lengths a_j = 3√λ_j" (pqac-00000012). The volume of this ellipsoid, (4/3)π∏a_j, provides a scalar summary of total uncertainty while retaining directional information that a single RMS number discards (pqac-00000012).

Alternatively, the ellipsoid can be computed analytically from the kinematic Jacobian. Issametova et al. explain: "Robot parameter or drive-error uncertainties are represented by a covariance matrix Σ_q and propagated through the kinematic Jacobian, using the relationship Σ_X = J_q Σ_q J_qᵀ" (pqac-00000002). The 3×3 translational block of Σ_X is then eigendecomposed to obtain the ellipsoid. For task-space error, Sinha and Chakraborty (preprint) show that joint-space uncertainty propagated through the position Jacobian J_p yields "δXᵀ(J_p J_pᵀ)⁻¹δX ≤ c," which "geometrically describes an ellipsoid" of position errors at the end-effector (pqac-00000030).

### 2.2 Protocol and Validation

Issametova et al. validated the ellipsoid approach experimentally on a **FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L**, measuring at "25 workspace points and 50 repeated trials per point, with a laser tracker accurate to about 0.01 mm" (pqac-00000015). They found that analytical and Monte Carlo ellipsoids agreed within 1–3% for compact and medium configurations, but diverged by 7–10% for elongated configurations where nonlinear kinematics dominate: "Experimental error ellipsoids showed that the major axis could be displaced by up to 10–11° relative to model predictions, with variance up to 20% higher than predicted" (pqac-00000039). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/math14030580).

Makhambetov et al. used a purely computational approach on a generic 6-DOF manipulator with "N = 10,000 trials across 50 workspace configurations" and rendered 3σ error ellipsoids through a Unity3D Digital Twin (pqac-00000031). Their ellipsoids were anisotropic, with the longest axis primarily vertical due to gravitational elastic deformation (pqac-00000014). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/electronics15143095) but contains no physical measurement validation; the authors note that "future work will compare them with measured end-effector scatter using a laser tracker" (pqac-00000019).

Rezala and Arbaoui used the stochastic ellipsoid method to analyze repeatability errors caused by joint friction variations, noting that "the stochastic ellipsoid method is able to generate repeatability predictions for the entire workspace" (pqac-00000035). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.5829/ije.2022.35.02b.21).

### 2.3 How to Repeat for Low-Cost Arms

For the AgileX PiPER or SO-101, one can command the arm to the same pose repeatedly (≥30 cycles per ISO 9283), record the TCP position using an AprilTag-based external camera system or a dial indicator, compute the 3×3 position covariance from the scatter, and eigendecompose it to obtain the ellipsoid axes and semi-lengths. This requires no laser tracker; the user's existing fixed cameras and AprilTags can serve as the measurement system, though with lower absolute accuracy than a laser tracker. **No published study has applied error ellipsoid analysis specifically to AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$2,000 arms.**

## 3. Probabilistic Workspace Maps

### 3.1 Monte Carlo Workspace Characterization

Workspace maps extend single-point ellipsoid analysis to the entire reachable space. Makhambetov et al. constructed a "probabilistic workspace map using 3,000 uniformly sampled configurations within joint limits and 500 trials per point, totaling 1,500,000 forward-kinematics evaluations" (pqac-00000012). The result is a color-coded 3D point cloud: "green denotes RMS error below 5 mm, yellow 5–15 mm, and red above 15 mm" (pqac-00000013). The maps reveal that "central workspace corresponds to compact configurations" with low error, while "reliability decreases toward workspace boundaries" (pqac-00000018).

Issametova et al. constructed a geometric-reliability map for the FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L, defining reliability as the probability that the end-effector lands within a tolerance region. They report "approximately 0.98 in central workspace regions associated with compact configurations" declining to "approximately 0.70 in peripheral zones" (pqac-00000039). This was computed from both analytical (Jacobian-based) and Monte Carlo methods, peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/math14030580).

### 3.2 Measurement-Based Workspace Maps

Chen applied the ISO 9283 protocol to the **Baxter** robot to generate "a 3D mapping of repeatability at different heights," finding that "repeatability generally deteriorated as the target moved farther from the robot" (pqac-00000000). The protocol tested 15 target locations at three heights, with 30 cycles per experiment repeated 30 times (900 measurements per location), using 3D dial gauges with 0.005 mm accuracy (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000027). This is a thesis (2015).

### 3.3 ISO 9283 Protocol Summary

The ISO 9283 standard prescribes the canonical measurement protocol. A test cube is placed in the most-used workspace region with edges parallel to the robot base coordinates. Five poses (P1–P5) lie on a diagonal test plane, P1 at the cube center and P2–P5 near diagonal corners. The robot visits these poses in unidirectional order through 30 cycles at each of three speeds (10%, 50%, 100% of rated velocity) and 100% rated payload. Position repeatability is computed as "RP_l = mean distance from the barycentre plus three standard deviations" (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000023). This protocol has been applied with various measurement tools including laser trackers (Faro Vantage, accuracy ±0.009 mm), contact gauges, and vision systems (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

## 4. Jacobian-Based Confidence Volumes and Error Along a Path

### 4.1 The Probabilistic Product-of-Exponentials (PPOE) Model

Meyer et al. presented the PPOE model at IROS 2022, which "does not only consider the robot's deterministic geometry but additionally models time-varying and configuration-dependent errors in a probabilistic way" (pqac-00000028). The model propagates errors along the kinematic chain using Lie-group operations and computes their influence on the end-effector pose. It was validated on a **Kinova Jaco2** arm, where "PPOE-based 2D estimation achieved mean lateral errors of 0.29 ± 0.15 cm and 0.50 ± 0.25 cm" compared with forward kinematics alone at "0.82 ± 0.49 cm and 1.48 ± 0.38 cm" (pqac-00000042). This is a peer-reviewed IEEE conference paper (DOI: 10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399).

### 4.2 pytransform3d: An Open-Source Uncertainty Visualization Library

The Python library pytransform3d provides the most accessible implementation for low-cost arm users. Fabisch and Popescu describe its uncertainty module: it "models uncertain rigid transformations using a transformation-matrix mean and a 6×6 covariance matrix over exponential coordinates" and supports "composition, inversion, and fusion of uncertain transformations" (pqac-00000008). Key functions include `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms(A2B, B2C, cov_A, cov_B)` for propagating joint-displacement covariances, and `adjoint_from_transform(A2B)` for transferring covariance between frames (pqac-00000011). The library renders "an equiprobable projected 6D pose hyperellipsoid at configurable kσ intervals in 3D; the example describes a 3σ hyperellipsoid, corresponding to 99.7% probability" (pqac-00000008). Importantly, the authors note that "an ellipsoid is not an appropriate representation" for all cases because rotation-translation coupling can produce banana-shaped distributions rather than ordinary ellipsoids (pqac-00000009). The library supports URDF loading through `UrdfTransformManager` and visualization through both Matplotlib and Open3D (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457).

### 4.3 Path-Error Visualization

For error along a path, Issametova et al. describe evaluating the Jacobian-based reliability calculation "along θ(t), allowing reliability, variance, or error to be plotted against path position or time; trajectory planners can constrain R(θ(t)) to remain above a required threshold" (pqac-00000002). ISO 9283 also defines path accuracy and path repeatability as separate criteria measured by recording the continuous trajectory and comparing it with the commanded path (pqac-00000020).

## 5. Calibration Context: Comparative Results Across Arm Models

While this review focuses on visualization rather than calibration, several papers provide comparative positioning-accuracy results that establish the baseline these visualizations would display:

- **FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L**: Positioning error increased from 0.018 mm (first 3 months) to 0.041 mm (last 3 months) in operational monitoring (pqac-00000039).
- **Kinova Jaco2**: Forward kinematics error of 0.82–1.48 cm, reduced to 0.29–0.50 cm with PPOE-based sensor fusion using AprilTags (pqac-00000042).
- **Franka Panda**: Mean absolute positioning error reduced from ~10 mm to 0.24–0.35 mm by MUKCa calibration; Kinova Gen3Lite improved from 5.99 mm to 2.66 mm, with remaining error attributed to "joint backlash in planetary gearboxes" (pqac-00000041). This is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2503.12584).
- **Generic 7-DOF arm** (Wyk et al., preprint): Bayesian remastering using a motion capture system reduced "the average robot positioning error to 0.26 mm" and the "average absolute positioning error" from over 4 mm (Vernier method) to "within 1.5 mm" with Bayesian zero-offset optimization (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034).
- **Kuka KR 16-2**: Tested per PN-EN 9283 with a Faro Vantage laser tracker (accuracy ±0.009 mm), 30 measurements per test configuration, robot warmed up with a 40-minute cycle (pqac-00000021).
- **Panasonic TM-2000**: ISO 9283 contact-measurement protocol, 1200 mm ISO cube, 5 points, 30 cycles, 50% max speed, 3 kg load, ambient 20–22°C (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026).

**No published study was found that applies error ellipsoid analysis, probabilistic workspace mapping, or ISO 9283 repeatability testing specifically to the AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$200 leader-follower arms.** The closest analogue is the Kinova Gen3Lite (~$5,000), which exhibited substantial backlash-related positioning error around 2–6 mm (pqac-00000041). Low-cost arms with hobby servos and planetary gearboxes are expected to show similar or larger non-Gaussian error distributions due to backlash and compliance.

## 6. Software Tools Summary

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

## 7. Practical Recommendations for Low-Cost Arms

For the user's AgileX PiPER and SO-101 arms with AprilTag-based measurement:

1. **Collect repeated TCP measurements** at ≥5 workspace locations following the ISO 9283 protocol (30 cycles per location, unidirectional approach). AprilTags detected by the fixed cameras provide the external position reference. Record raw 3D coordinates.

2. **Compute error ellipsoids** at each location using NumPy: subtract the mean, form the 3×3 covariance matrix, and eigendecompose. Plot 3σ ellipsoids using Matplotlib or Open3D. The eigenvalues reveal whether error is isotropic or dominated by a particular direction (e.g., gravity-axis compliance).

3. **Build a workspace map** by repeating step 1 across a grid of reachable locations. Color-code each point by its RMS repeatability and render as a 3D scatter plot. This requires no laser tracker and can be performed with the existing camera infrastructure.

4. **Use pytransform3d** for Jacobian-based propagation if a URDF model of the arm is available. The `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms` function propagates joint-angle covariances through the kinematic chain, and the projected hyperellipsoid visualization shows the resulting end-effector uncertainty (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011).

5. **Plot path error** by commanding a straight-line or circular trajectory, recording the measured TCP path at high frequency, and computing cross-track and along-track deviations as a function of path parameter. ISO 9283 path repeatability compares the envelope of deviations across multiple traversals (pqac-00000020).

## 8. Gaps in Published Evidence

- No peer-reviewed study applies error ellipsoid or probabilistic workspace mapping to the AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$200 robot arms.
- No published software provides a turnkey, one-click repeatability map function; assembly from numerical primitives is required (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000019).
- The Makhambetov et al. (2026) workspace maps and error ellipsoids are simulation-only and have not been validated against physical measurements (pqac-00000019).
- Path-error visualization (error plotted continuously along a trajectory rather than at discrete points) is described mathematically but not demonstrated with dedicated software in the retrieved literature (pqac-00000002).
- The Sinha and Chakraborty (2019) robust IK work with error ellipsoids is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.1910.10852) and has not appeared in a peer-reviewed venue (pqac-00000030).
- The Franzese et al. (2025) MUKCa calibration study for Franka, KUKA, and Kinova is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2503.12584) (pqac-00000041)."}

Five poses (P1–P5) lie on a diagonal test plane, P1 at the cube center and P2–P5 near diagonal corners. The robot visits these poses in unidirectional order through 30 cycles at each of three speeds (10%, 50%, 100% of rated velocity) and 100% rated payload. Position repeatability is computed as "RP_l = mean distance from the barycentre plus three standard deviations" (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000023). This protocol has been applied with various measurement tools including laser trackers (Faro Vantage, accuracy ±0.009 mm), contact gauges, and vision systems (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

## 4. Jacobian-Based Confidence Volumes and Error Along a Path

### 4.1 The Probabilistic Product-of-Exponentials (PPOE) Model

Meyer et al. presented the PPOE model at IROS 2022, which "does not only consider the robot's deterministic geometry but additionally models time-varying and configuration-dependent errors in a probabilistic way" (pqac-00000028). The model propagates errors along the kinematic chain using Lie-group operations and computes their influence on the end-effector pose. It was validated on a **Kinova Jaco2** arm, where "PPOE-based 2D estimation achieved mean lateral errors of 0.29 ± 0.15 cm and 0.50 ± 0.25 cm" compared with forward kinematics alone at "0.82 ± 0.49 cm and 1.48 ± 0.38 cm" (pqac-00000042). This is a peer-reviewed IEEE conference paper (DOI: 10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399).

### 4.2 pytransform3d: An Open-Source Uncertainty Visualization Library

The Python library pytransform3d provides the most accessible implementation for low-cost arm users. Fabisch and Popescu describe its uncertainty module: it "models uncertain rigid transformations using a transformation-matrix mean and a 6×6 covariance matrix over exponential coordinates" and supports "composition, inversion, and fusion of uncertain transformations" (pqac-00000008). Key functions include `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms(A2B, B2C, cov_A, cov_B)` for propagating joint-displacement covariances, and `adjoint_from_transform(A2B)` for transferring covariance between frames (pqac-00000011). The library renders "an equiprobable projected 6D pose hyperellipsoid at configurable kσ intervals in 3D; the example describes a 3σ hyperellipsoid, corresponding to 99.7% probability" (pqac-00000008). Importantly, the authors note that "an ellipsoid is not an appropriate representation" for all cases because rotation-translation coupling can produce banana-shaped distributions rather than ordinary ellipsoids (pqac-00000009). The library supports URDF loading through `UrdfTransformManager` and visualization through both Matplotlib and Open3D (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457).

### 4.3 Path-Error Visualization

For error along a path, Issametova et al. describe evaluating the Jacobian-based reliability calculation "along θ(t), allowing reliability, variance, or error to be plotted against path position or time; trajectory planners can constrain R(θ(t)) to remain above a required threshold" (pqac-00000002). ISO 9283 also defines path accuracy and path repeatability as separate criteria measured by recording the continuous trajectory and comparing it with the commanded path (pqac-00000020).

## 5. Calibration Context: Comparative Results Across Arm Models

While this review focuses on visualization rather than calibration, several papers provide comparative positioning-accuracy results that establish the baseline these visualizations would display:

- **FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L**: Positioning error increased from 0.018 mm (first 3 months) to 0.041 mm (last 3 months) in operational monitoring (pqac-00000039).
- **Kinova Jaco2**: Forward kinematics error of 0.82–1.48 cm, reduced to 0.29–0.50 cm with PPOE-based sensor fusion using AprilTags (pqac-00000042).
- **Franka Panda**: Mean absolute positioning error reduced from ~10 mm to 0.24–0.35 mm by MUKCa calibration; Kinova Gen3Lite improved from 5.99 mm to 2.66 mm, with remaining error attributed to "joint backlash in planetary gearboxes" (pqac-00000041). This is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2503.12584).
- **Generic 7-DOF arm** (Wyk et al., preprint): Bayesian remastering using a motion capture system reduced "the average robot positioning error to 0.26 mm" and the "average absolute positioning error" from over 4 mm (Vernier method) to "within 1.5 mm" with Bayesian zero-offset optimization (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034).
- **Kuka KR 16-2**: Tested per PN-EN 9283 with a Faro Vantage laser tracker (accuracy ±0.009 mm), 30 measurements per test configuration, robot warmed up with a 40-minute cycle (pqac-00000021).
- **Panasonic TM-2000**: ISO 9283 contact-measurement protocol, 1200 mm ISO cube, 5 points, 30 cycles, 50% max speed, 3 kg load, ambient 20–22°C (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026).

**No published study was found that applies error ellipsoid analysis, probabilistic workspace mapping, or ISO 9283 repeatability testing specifically to the AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$200 leader-follower arms.** The closest analogue is the Kinova Gen3Lite (~$5,000), which exhibited substantial backlash-related positioning error around 2–6 mm (pqac-00000041). Low-cost arms with hobby servos and planetary gearboxes are expected to show similar or larger non-Gaussian error distributions due to backlash and compliance.

## 6. Software Tools Summary

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

## 7. Practical Recommendations for Low-Cost Arms

For the user's AgileX PiPER and SO-101 arms with AprilTag-based measurement:

1. **Collect repeated TCP measurements** at ≥5 workspace locations following the ISO 9283 protocol (30 cycles per location, unidirectional approach). AprilTags detected by the fixed cameras provide the external position reference. Record raw 3D coordinates.

2. **Compute error ellipsoids** at each location using NumPy: subtract the mean, form the 3×3 covariance matrix, and eigendecompose. Plot 3σ ellipsoids using Matplotlib or Open3D. The eigenvalues reveal whether error is isotropic or dominated by a particular direction (e.g., gravity-axis compliance).

3. **Build a workspace map** by repeating step 1 across a grid of reachable locations. Color-code each point by its RMS repeatability and render as a 3D scatter plot. This requires no laser tracker and can be performed with the existing camera infrastructure.

4. **Use pytransform3d** for Jacobian-based propagation if a URDF model of the arm is available. The `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms` function propagates joint-angle covariances through the kinematic chain, and the projected hyperellipsoid visualization shows the resulting end-effector uncertainty (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011).

5. **Plot path error** by commanding a straight-line or circular trajectory, recording the measured TCP path at high frequency, and computing cross-track and along-track deviations as a function of path parameter. ISO 9283 path repeatability compares the envelope of deviations across multiple traversals (pqac-00000020).

## 8. Gaps in Published Evidence

- No peer-reviewed study applies error ellipsoid or probabilistic workspace mapping to the AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$200 robot arms.
- No published software provides a turnkey, one-click repeatability map function; assembly from numerical primitives is required (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000019).
- The Makhambetov et al. (2026) workspace maps and error ellipsoids are simulation-only and have not been validated against physical measurements (pqac-00000019).
- Path-error visualization (error plotted continuously along a trajectory rather than at discrete points) is described mathematically but not demonstrated with dedicated software in the retrieved literature (pqac-00000002).
- The Sinha and Chakraborty (2019) robust IK work with error ellipsoids is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.1910.10852) and has not appeared in a peer-reviewed venue (pqac-00000030).
- The Franzese et al. (2025) MUKCa calibration study for Franka, KUKA, and Kinova is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2503.12584) (pqac-00000041)."}

## 2. Error Ellipsoids (Stochastic Ellipsoid Method)

### 2.1 Mathematical Construction

The stochastic ellipsoid method represents positioning uncertainty at a given robot configuration as a three-dimensional confidence region derived from the covariance of end-effector position errors. Makhambetov et al. describe the procedure: "The displacement samples are calculated as Δp = p_noisy − p_nom, then their covariance matrix Σ is eigendecomposed as Σ = VDVᵀ. The eigenvectors in V define the principal directions of the uncertainty ellipsoid, while the eigenvalues λ_j represent variances along those directions. A 3σ ellipsoid uses semi-axis lengths a_j = 3√λ_j" (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 5-7). The volume of this ellipsoid, (4/3)π∏a_j, provides a scalar summary of total uncertainty while retaining directional information that a single RMS number discards (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 5-7).

Alternatively, the ellipsoid can be computed analytically from the kinematic Jacobian. Issametova et al. explain: "Robot parameter or drive-error uncertainties are represented by a covariance matrix Σ_q and propagated through the kinematic Jacobian, using the relationship Σ_X = J_q Σ_q J_qᵀ" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 48-49). The 3×3 translational block of Σ_X is then eigendecomposed to obtain the ellipsoid. For task-space error, Sinha and Chakraborty (preprint) show that joint-space uncertainty propagated through the position Jacobian J_p yields "δXᵀ(J_p J_pᵀ)⁻¹δX ≤ c," which "geometrically describes an ellipsoid" of position errors at the end-effector (sinha2019computingrobustinverse pages 3-4).

### 2.2 Protocol and Validation

Issametova et al. validated the ellipsoid approach experimentally on a **FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L**, measuring at "25 workspace points and 50 repeated trials per point, with a laser tracker accurate to about 0.01 mm" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 37-39). They found that analytical and Monte Carlo ellipsoids agreed within 1–3% for compact and medium configurations, but diverged by 7–10% for elongated configurations where nonlinear kinematics dominate: "Experimental error ellipsoids showed that the major axis could be displaced by up to 10–11° relative to model predictions, with variance up to 20% higher than predicted" (issametova2026reliabilityinrobotics pages 45-48). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/math14030580).

Makhambetov et al. used a purely computational approach on a generic 6-DOF manipulator with "N = 10,000 trials across 50 workspace configurations" and rendered 3σ error ellipsoids through a Unity3D Digital Twin (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 1-2). Their ellipsoids were anisotropic, with the longest axis primarily vertical due to gravitational elastic deformation (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 11-14). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/electronics15143095) but contains no physical measurement validation; the authors note that "future work will compare them with measured end-effector scatter using a laser tracker" (makhambetov2026stochasticpositioningaccuracy pages 16-17).

Rezala and Arbaoui used the stochastic ellipsoid method to analyze repeatability errors caused by joint friction variations, noting that "the stochastic ellipsoid method is able to generate repeatability predictions for the entire workspace" (rezala2022analysisrandoncauses pages 2-4). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.5829/ije.2022.35.02b.21).

### 2.3 How to Repeat for Low-Cost Arms

For the AgileX PiPER or SO-101, one can command the arm to the same pose repeatedly (≥30 cycles per ISO 9283), record the TCP position using an AprilTag-based external camera system or a dial indicator, compute the 3×3 position covariance from the scatter, and eigendecompose it to obtain the ellipsoid axes and semi-lengths. This requires no laser tracker; the user's existing fixed cameras and AprilTags can serve as the measurement system, though with lower absolute accuracy than a laser tracker. **No published study has applied error ellipsoid analysis specifically to AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$2,000 arms.**

# Visualizing Robot Positioning Accuracy and Repeatability in 3D

## 1. Overview

Three principal methods appear in the published literature for showing a robot's positioning accuracy and repeatability in three dimensions: **(1) error ellipsoids** (the stochastic ellipsoid method), **(2) probabilistic workspace maps**, and **(3) Jacobian-based confidence volumes along a path or trajectory**. Each can be computed from physical measurements, from modeled parameter uncertainties, or from both. The table below summarizes these methods, their mathematical basis, published protocols, and supporting software.

Orientation shows principal error directions, semi-axis lengths show directional dispersion, and volume summarizes overall uncertainty. | From measured or simulated Cartesian errors, compute covariance Σ and eigendecompose it as Σ = VDVᵀ. Eigenvectors give principal directions and eigenvalues λ_j give variances. A 3σ ellipsoid has semi-axes a_j = 3√λ_j. Joint-space uncertainty can also be propagated into task space through the Jacobian. ## 2. Error Ellipsoids (Stochastic Ellipsoid Method)

### 2.1 Mathematical Construction

The stochastic ellipsoid method represents positioning uncertainty at a given robot configuration as a three-dimensional confidence region derived from the covariance of end-effector position errors. Makhambetov et al. describe the procedure: "The displacement samples are calculated as Δp = p_noisy − p_nom, then their covariance matrix Σ is eigendecomposed as Σ = VDVᵀ. The eigenvectors in V define the principal directions of the uncertainty ellipsoid, while the eigenvalues λ_j represent variances along those directions. A 3σ ellipsoid uses semi-axis lengths a_j = 3√λ_j" (pqac-00000012). The volume of this ellipsoid, (4/3)π∏a_j, provides a scalar summary of total uncertainty while retaining directional information that a single RMS number discards (pqac-00000012).

Alternatively, the ellipsoid can be computed analytically from the kinematic Jacobian. Issametova et al. explain: "Robot parameter or drive-error uncertainties are represented by a covariance matrix Σ_q and propagated through the kinematic Jacobian, using the relationship Σ_X = J_q Σ_q J_qᵀ" (pqac-00000002). The 3×3 translational block of Σ_X is then eigendecomposed to obtain the ellipsoid. For task-space error, Sinha and Chakraborty (preprint) show that joint-space uncertainty propagated through the position Jacobian J_p yields "δXᵀ(J_p J_pᵀ)⁻¹δX ≤ c," which "geometrically describes an ellipsoid" of position errors at the end-effector (pqac-00000030).

### 2.2 Protocol and Validation

Issametova et al. validated the ellipsoid approach experimentally on a **FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L**, measuring at "25 workspace points and 50 repeated trials per point, with a laser tracker accurate to about 0.01 mm" (pqac-00000015). They found that analytical and Monte Carlo ellipsoids agreed within 1–3% for compact and medium configurations, but diverged by 7–10% for elongated configurations where nonlinear kinematics dominate: "Experimental error ellipsoids showed that the major axis could be displaced by up to 10–11° relative to model predictions, with variance up to 20% higher than predicted" (pqac-00000039). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/math14030580).

Makhambetov et al. used a purely computational approach on a generic 6-DOF manipulator with "N = 10,000 trials across 50 workspace configurations" and rendered 3σ error ellipsoids through a Unity3D Digital Twin (pqac-00000031). Their ellipsoids were anisotropic, with the longest axis primarily vertical due to gravitational elastic deformation (pqac-00000014). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/electronics15143095) but contains no physical measurement validation; the authors note that "future work will compare them with measured end-effector scatter using a laser tracker" (pqac-00000019).

Rezala and Arbaoui used the stochastic ellipsoid method to analyze repeatability errors caused by joint friction variations, noting that "the stochastic ellipsoid method is able to generate repeatability predictions for the entire workspace" (pqac-00000035). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.5829/ije.2022.35.02b.21).

### 2.3 How to Repeat for Low-Cost Arms

For the AgileX PiPER or SO-101, one can command the arm to the same pose repeatedly (≥30 cycles per ISO 9283), record the TCP position using an AprilTag-based external camera system or a dial indicator, compute the 3×3 position covariance from the scatter, and eigendecompose it to obtain the ellipsoid axes and semi-lengths. This requires no laser tracker; the user's existing fixed cameras and AprilTags can serve as the measurement system, though with lower absolute accuracy than a laser tracker. **No published study has applied error ellipsoid analysis specifically to AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$2,000 arms.**

## 3. Probabilistic Workspace Maps

### 3.1 Monte Carlo Workspace Characterization

Workspace maps extend single-point ellipsoid analysis to the entire reachable space. Makhambetov et al. constructed a "probabilistic workspace map using 3,000 uniformly sampled configurations within joint limits and 500 trials per point, totaling 1,500,000 forward-kinematics evaluations" (pqac-00000012). The result is a color-coded 3D point cloud: "green denotes RMS error below 5 mm, yellow 5–15 mm, and red above 15 mm" (pqac-00000013). The maps reveal that "central workspace corresponds to compact configurations" with low error, while "reliability decreases toward workspace boundaries" (pqac-00000018).

Issametova et al. constructed a geometric-reliability map for the FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L, defining reliability as the probability that the end-effector lands within a tolerance region. They report "approximately 0.98 in central workspace regions associated with compact configurations" declining to "approximately 0.70 in peripheral zones" (pqac-00000039). This was computed from both analytical (Jacobian-based) and Monte Carlo methods, peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3390/math14030580).

### 3.2 Measurement-Based Workspace Maps

Chen applied the ISO 9283 protocol to the **Baxter** robot to generate "a 3D mapping of repeatability at different heights," finding that "repeatability generally deteriorated as the target moved farther from the robot" (pqac-00000000). The protocol tested 15 target locations at three heights, with 30 cycles per experiment repeated 30 times (900 measurements per location), using 3D dial gauges with 0.005 mm accuracy (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000027). This is a thesis (2015).

### 3.3 ISO 9283 Protocol Summary

The ISO 9283 standard prescribes the canonical measurement protocol. A test cube is placed in the most-used workspace region with edges parallel to the robot base coordinates. Five poses (P1–P5) lie on a diagonal test plane, P1 at the cube center and P2–P5 near diagonal corners. The robot visits these poses in unidirectional order through 30 cycles at each of three speeds (10%, 50%, 100% of rated velocity) and 100% rated payload. Position repeatability is computed as "RP_l = mean distance from the barycentre plus three standard deviations" (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000023). This protocol has been applied with various measurement tools including laser trackers (Faro Vantage, accuracy ±0.009 mm), contact gauges, and vision systems (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

## 4. Jacobian-Based Confidence Volumes and Error Along a Path

### 4.1 The Probabilistic Product-of-Exponentials (PPOE) Model

Meyer et al. presented the PPOE model at IROS 2022, which "does not only consider the robot's deterministic geometry but additionally models time-varying and configuration-dependent errors in a probabilistic way" (pqac-00000028). The model propagates errors along the kinematic chain using Lie-group operations and computes their influence on the end-effector pose. It was validated on a **Kinova Jaco2** arm, where "PPOE-based 2D estimation achieved mean lateral errors of 0.29 ± 0.15 cm and 0.50 ± 0.25 cm" compared with forward kinematics alone at "0.82 ± 0.49 cm and 1.48 ± 0.38 cm" (pqac-00000042). This is a peer-reviewed IEEE conference paper (DOI: 10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981399).

### 4.2 pytransform3d: An Open-Source Uncertainty Visualization Library

The Python library pytransform3d provides the most accessible implementation for low-cost arm users. Fabisch and Popescu describe its uncertainty module: it "models uncertain rigid transformations using a transformation-matrix mean and a 6×6 covariance matrix over exponential coordinates" and supports "composition, inversion, and fusion of uncertain transformations" (pqac-00000008). Key functions include `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms(A2B, B2C, cov_A, cov_B)` for propagating joint-displacement covariances, and `adjoint_from_transform(A2B)` for transferring covariance between frames (pqac-00000011). The library renders "an equiprobable projected 6D pose hyperellipsoid at configurable kσ intervals in 3D; the example describes a 3σ hyperellipsoid, corresponding to 99.7% probability" (pqac-00000008). Importantly, the authors note that "an ellipsoid is not an appropriate representation" for all cases because rotation-translation coupling can produce banana-shaped distributions rather than ordinary ellipsoids (pqac-00000009). The library supports URDF loading through `UrdfTransformManager` and visualization through both Matplotlib and Open3D (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). This is a peer-reviewed journal article (DOI: 10.3389/frobt.2026.1860457).

### 4.3 Path-Error Visualization

For error along a path, Issametova et al. describe evaluating the Jacobian-based reliability calculation "along θ(t), allowing reliability, variance, or error to be plotted against path position or time; trajectory planners can constrain R(θ(t)) to remain above a required threshold" (pqac-00000002). ISO 9283 also defines path accuracy and path repeatability as separate criteria measured by recording the continuous trajectory and comparing it with the commanded path (pqac-00000020).

## 5. Calibration Context: Comparative Results Across Arm Models

While this review focuses on visualization rather than calibration, several papers provide comparative positioning-accuracy results that establish the baseline these visualizations would display:

- **FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L**: Positioning error increased from 0.018 mm (first 3 months) to 0.041 mm (last 3 months) in operational monitoring (pqac-00000039).
- **Kinova Jaco2**: Forward kinematics error of 0.82–1.48 cm, reduced to 0.29–0.50 cm with PPOE-based sensor fusion using AprilTags (pqac-00000042).
- **Franka Panda**: Mean absolute positioning error reduced from ~10 mm to 0.24–0.35 mm by MUKCa calibration; Kinova Gen3Lite improved from 5.99 mm to 2.66 mm, with remaining error attributed to "joint backlash in planetary gearboxes" (pqac-00000041). - **Kuka KR 16-2**: Tested per PN-EN 9283 with a Faro Vantage laser tracker (accuracy ±0.009 mm), 30 measurements per test configuration, robot warmed up with a 40-minute cycle (pqac-00000021).
- **Panasonic TM-2000**: ISO 9283 contact-measurement protocol, 1200 mm ISO cube, 5 points, 30 cycles, 50% max speed, 3 kg load, ambient 20–22°C (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026).

*Table: Software and computational frameworks for turning measured or modeled robot-position errors into ellipsoids, workspace maps, and trajectory-error displays. The notes distinguish turnkey visualization features from tools that require custom statistical processing.*

## 7. Practical Recommendations for Low-Cost Arms

For the user's AgileX PiPER and SO-101 arms with AprilTag-based measurement:

1. **Collect repeated TCP measurements** at ≥5 workspace locations following the ISO 9283 protocol (30 cycles per location, unidirectional approach). AprilTags detected by the fixed cameras provide the external position reference. Record raw 3D coordinates.

2. **Compute error ellipsoids** at each location using NumPy: subtract the mean, form the 3×3 covariance matrix, and eigendecompose. Plot 3σ ellipsoids using Matplotlib or Open3D. The eigenvalues reveal whether error is isotropic or dominated by a particular direction (e.g., gravity-axis compliance).

3. **Build a workspace map** by repeating step 1 across a grid of reachable locations. Color-code each point by its RMS repeatability and render as a 3D scatter plot. This requires no laser tracker and can be performed with the existing camera infrastructure.

4. **Use pytransform3d** for Jacobian-based propagation if a URDF model of the arm is available. The `concat_locally_uncertain_transforms` function propagates joint-angle covariances through the kinematic chain, and the projected hyperellipsoid visualization shows the resulting end-effector uncertainty (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011).

5. **Plot path error** by commanding a straight-line or circular trajectory, recording the measured TCP path at high frequency, and computing cross-track and along-track deviations as a function of path parameter. ISO 9283 path repeatability compares the envelope of deviations across multiple traversals (pqac-00000020).

## 8. Gaps in Published Evidence

- No peer-reviewed study applies error ellipsoid or probabilistic workspace mapping to the AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or comparable sub-$200 robot arms.
- No published software provides a turnkey, one-click repeatability map function; assembly from numerical primitives is required (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000019).
- The Makhambetov et al. (2026) workspace maps and error ellipsoids are simulation-only and have not been validated against physical measurements (pqac-00000019).
- Path-error visualization (error plotted continuously along a trajectory rather than at discrete points) is described mathematically but not demonstrated with dedicated software in the retrieved literature (pqac-00000002).
- The Sinha and Chakraborty (2019) robust IK work with error ellipsoids is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.1910.10852) and has not appeared in a peer-reviewed venue (pqac-00000030).
- The Franzese et al. (2025) MUKCa calibration study for Franka, KUKA, and Kinova is a preprint (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2503.12584) (pqac-00000041).

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a probabilistic, Jacobian-based approach for visualizing robot positioning accuracy and repeatability in 3D. Robot parameter or drive-error uncertainties are represented by a covariance matrix Σq and propagated through the kinematic Jacobian, using the relationship ΣX = JqΣqJqT. The resulting Cartesian covariance can be visualized as 3D error ellipsoids, whose size and orientation reflect positioning uncertainty. Applying this calculation throughout sampled joint configurations or workspace points produces a geometric reliability or repeatability map: central, compact configurations generally show higher reliability, while peripheral regions show lower reliability because Jacobian coefficients and sensitivity to parameter errors increase. Reliability is defined probabilistically as R = P(X ∈ Ω), where Ω is the acceptable positioning tolerance region. For trajectory analysis, the same calculation is evaluated along θ(t), allowing reliability, variance, or error to be plotted against path position or time; trajectory planners can constrain R(θ(t)) to remain above a required threshold. The excerpt does not identify a dedicated visualization software package. It mentions compatibility with modern FANUC control systems and recommends using reliability maps for workspace screening, configuration selection, trajectory optimization, and recalibration triggering. The framework is also extensible to mobile, redundant, parallel, and collaborative robots when their kinematics and uncertainty models are available.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a MATLAB-based workflow for processing and evaluating 3D robot positioning measurements, but it does not specify software or algorithms for visualizing error ellipsoids, workspace-wide repeatability maps, or error along a continuous path. In Phase 1, three surface-contact coordinates were reconstructed geometrically in MATLAB to estimate the end-effector’s sphere center. Thirty repeated measurements were compared with the overall mean center, and Euclidean distances between each measured center and that mean were calculated. These deviations were summarized using the mean deviation, standard deviation, and ISO-style repeatability measure RP_l = mean deviation + 3σ. In the vision-based phases, a calibrated external multi-camera tracking system captured and exported 3D positions for repeated robot trials. The measurements were processed into the same statistical indicators. For the ISO 9283 cube test, these metrics were computed independently at five spatial positions, enabling comparison of repeatability at different workspace locations; one position showed substantially larger variability. Thus, the excerpt supports computation from measured 3D coordinates using geometric reconstruction, mean-center comparison, Euclidean error, and statistical aggregation. It does not provide robot-parameter-based propagation, covariance/error-ellipsoid construction, graphical repeatability maps, or path-wise error calculations.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents pytransform3d’s tools for propagating and visualizing uncertainty in robot-arm transformations, but it does not discuss RoboDK or the MATLAB Robotics Toolbox. pytransform3d implements uncertainty propagation for SE(3) poses, including composition of uncertain transformations in a global reference frame through concat_globally_uncertain_transforms(A2B, cov_A2B, B2C, cov_B2C). Covariances can be associated with transformations using Cholesky decomposition, and uncertainty is accumulated as poses are concatenated. For visualization, the article explains that 6D transformation uncertainty must be projected into 3D; this can produce banana-like distributions rather than ordinary ellipsoids because rotation and translation interact. pytransform3d extends Matplotlib’s 3D plotting capabilities to display coordinate frames, arrows, cameras, transformation graphs, URDF models, primitive geometries, and meshes. Open3D supplies animation and static 3D visualization through a high-level interface resembling Matplotlib, while supporting the extended visualization functions. URDF support is provided through UrdfTransformManager, which loads robot descriptions and displays collision objects or visual geometry; joints can be configured with set_joint("joint_name", joint_angle), and transformations can then be requested for forward kinematics. ROS is mentioned only as the source/context for the URDF format, not as a separate error-ellipsoid or repeatability-map implementation. Repeatability maps are not described in this excerpt.
